study_design_identified: Observational analytical cross-sectional geospatial study
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: WAIT
selection_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: The study covers the full population of agricultural irrigation districts (excluding domestic, municipal, and water conservation agencies) and all DWR-mapped disadvantaged community census places (n = 97 ID-DACs; n = 56 GDCs) on the San Joaquin Valley floor across eight counties, limiting sampling bias, though total district sample size is omitted from the main text and boundary vintages differ for Kings County (2015 DWR vs. updated LAFCO).
measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: Groundwater reliance is not metered directly but modeled via a residual water-balance deficit combining 2016 Land IQ crop water requirements with 2001–2015 average surface water deliveries (2008–2019 or 2005–2019 for three districts), while imputing 'no record' surface water deliveries as zero. Community outcomes link census-tract-level CalEnviroScreen 4.0 percentiles to DAC census-place centroids, creating ecological/modifiable areal unit measurement error.
confounding: High concern: Neither the irrigation district era/water-right comparisons nor the ID-DAC (n = 97) versus GDC (n = 56) socioeconomic and environmental comparisons adjust for confounding variables such as Valley sub-region and hydrogeology, community population size (mean 9,899 vs. 20,515, p = 0.0035), municipal incorporation or domestic water-system infrastructure, or soil/crop suitability.
attrition: Low concern / Not applicable to cross-sectional design, though missing administrative data had material handling limitations: districts with 'no record' of surface water deliveries were imputed as receiving zero deliveries rather than excluded or subjected to sensitivity bounds, and Kings County lacked updated LAFCO boundaries (substituted with 2015 DWR boundaries).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is reported. While datasets and R scripts are publicly archived on Dryad and GitHub, the manuscript text omits the total sample size of analyzed irrigation districts, omits sample sizes for two of the five clusters (GDV and CCB), omits dispersion statistics (medians, IQRs, SDs) in Table 1, and omits methodological details of the cluster analysis (clustering algorithm, distance metric, and cluster-count selection criteria).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (moderate concern for spatial edge cases): Legal and institutional exposures—district formation eras, pre-1914 senior vs. post-1914 junior appropriative surface water rights, pending petitions, and surface water allocations—were compiled from official administrative registries (SWRCB eWRIMS, USBR contracts, GSPs, AWMPs, county LAFCOs) and verified with district managers; however, Kings County used 2015 DWR boundaries, DAC jurisdiction was assigned via census-place centroids rather than polygon overlap, and agricultural irrigation districts generally do not hold statutory domestic drinking-water mandates.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate: District groundwater deficit relies on asynchronous land-use (2016) and delivery (2001–2015) inputs, assumes zero lateral groundwater outflow, and treats missing delivery records as zero deliveries. Community drinking-water and groundwater-threat indicators rely on census-tract composite percentiles from CalEnviroScreen 4.0 matched to place centroids rather than direct community water-system or household tap-water measurements.
where_found: WAIT

study_design_identified: Cluster-randomized controlled trial (30 villages in Kampong Chhnang province stratified by commune climate vulnerability and randomized 15:15 to targeted 50% latrine subsidy vs. retail-price sales pitches; N = 2,821 retained household presentations), supplemented by 13 qualitative stakeholder interviews and a pilot cost-scalability analysis
why_tool_chosen: The primary causal design testing the study's main research questions is a cluster-randomized controlled trial in which 30 rural Cambodian villages were randomized as clusters (via Stata's randtreat) to receive targeted latrine subsidies versus unsubsidized retail sales pitches. Although the study also conducted 13 key-informant interviews (with sales agents, local authorities, and latrine business owners) and a cost analysis to contextualize implementation and scalability, the qualitative component serves as an embedded process check without standalone qualitative findings tables or participant quotations in the main text. Selecting 'RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)' directly captures the trial's defining cluster-specific methodological risk—Domain 1b (post-randomization identification and differential recruitment of IDPoor households within clusters by unblinded sales agents and village leaders)—alongside cluster randomization, post-hoc repeat-visit exclusions, and proxy order measurement.
selection_bias: High — Villages (30 clusters) were randomized prior to individual household identification, after which unblinded iDE sales agents worked with village authorities and neighbors to locate households without a toilet when a decisionmaker was home. Incentivized by commissions and subsidy availability, village authorities and sales agents more actively targeted poor households in treatment villages, generating a statistically significant imbalance in overall eligibility (51–52% treatment vs. 45% control, p = 0.00) driven by 5% more IDPoor households in treatment clusters (p = 0.00).
measurement_bias: Some concerns — The outcome measured initial latrine purchase orders recorded at the sales presentation by unblinded, commissioned iDE sales agents rather than verified physical latrine installations (10–20% of orders typically cancel prior to installation and were not tracked). Household-level climate vulnerability was also assessed via a single subjective 1-year recall question during subsidy screening, although 10% M&E spot checks of purchasing households and inspection for bunching at PPI cutoffs mitigated deliberate score manipulation.
confounding: Some concerns — Village-level cluster randomization (stratified by commune climate vulnerability) and regression controls for community and household climate vulnerability were used, but post-randomization recruitment differentially enrolled 5 percentage points more IDPoor households in treatment villages than control villages (p = 0.00), introducing potential residual socioeconomic and motivational confounding in village-level uptake regressions and subgroup comparisons.
attrition: Some concerns — Immediate sales pitch conversion decisions were recorded on the spot for 2,821 retained household presentations, but 1,598 duplicate-visit responses (including 36 latrine sales) were excluded post hoc to mimic single-visit conditions, village-level non-contact denominators (households without a toilet where no decisionmaker was home) were not reported, and post-order follow-up to actual physical installation was omitted despite typical 10–20% cancellation rates.
reporting_bias: Some concerns — No trial pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is cited; cluster baseline balance tables, full regression outputs, standard errors, and sensitivity analyses retaining the 1,598 excluded duplicate visits are omitted from the main text (deferred to Supporting Information), and minor numerical inconsistencies appear across pages (51% vs. close to 52% treatment eligibility; 26 vs. 29 repeat-visit subsidized sales).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / Adequate — Administrative targeting combined official Cambodian state classifications—specifically household IDPoor proxy-means registration and National Council for Sustainable Development commune-level Climate Vulnerability Index (CVI) tiers—with the validated 10-item Cambodia Poverty Probability Index (PPI). However, exact PPI thresholds and CVI score cutoffs were relegated to Supporting Information, household climate shock exposure relied on a single unverified self-report item, and qualitative interviews documented persistent misunderstandings of eligibility rules among sales agents and village leaders.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / Some concerns — Although framed around 'access to resilient sanitation', the trial measured only initial purchase orders ('Easy Latrine' or elevated 'Sky Latrine') at the point of pitch, without verifying latrine delivery, construction, order cancellation (typically 10–20%), structural flood performance, or sustained household use.
where_found: Design & overview: Abstract (p. 1), Introduction & Research Objectives (pp. 2–3). Eligibility operationalization (IDPoor, PPI, commune CVI, household climate recall): Methods (pp. 3–4). Cluster randomization, sample size, qualitative stakeholder sample, field sales procedures, M&E spot checks, and duplicate-visit exclusions: Methods (p. 4 & fns. 15–17). Regression specifications & qualitative coding: Data analysis (pp. 5–6). Uptake, subgroup, and market-distortion findings (including IDPoor eligibility imbalance): Results & Table 1 (pp. 6–8). Order cancellations, single-province scope, post-randomization targeting bias, subjective climate item, and agent PPI misunderstandings: Limitations & Recommendations (pp. 8–10).

study_design_identified: Multi-level factorial cluster-randomized controlled trial (76 slums / 152-153 slum clusters in Mumbai randomized to slum-level political coordination and cluster-level bureaucratic assistance, with 1-year midline and 5-year endline household surveys, supplemented by 9 qualitative stakeholder interviews for mechanism illustration)
why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical strategy is a two-stage factorial cluster-randomized controlled trial in which 76 slums were block-randomized to political coordination (T2) and 152 slum clusters within those slums were cluster-randomized to bureaucratic assistance (T1) (PDF pp. 3, 17-20). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, "RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)" is the exact dedicated checklist for cluster-randomized trials. Although Appendix H includes brief illustrative insights from NGO progress reports and 9 semi-structured stakeholder interviews (6 NGO workers, 2 BMC engineers, 1 corporator) to contextualize mechanisms, the study is framed and executed as a quantitative field experiment rather than an integrated mixed-methods study, making the cluster-RCT RoB 2 variant strictly more appropriate and diagnostic than MMAT.
selection_bias: Some concerns: Although the 76 study slums were purposively sampled via a pre-baseline mapping exercise, baseline households were selected via random walk with pre-specified eligibility screening prior to randomization (PDF pp. 18-19, 51). One cluster of 153 was dropped in Step 2 randomization, with robustness verified under alternative assignments (Table S17, PDF p. 73). However, 2,444 of the 6,652 endline observations (36.7%) were replacement households recruited via random walk after interventions had concluded, and endline results restricted exclusively to the pre-randomization baseline cohort are not separately reported.
measurement_bias: Low concern for the primary outcome; some concerns for secondary/intermediate outcomes: Primary endline formalization (Formalized) required independent survey enumerators to physically inspect both the household's BMC water pipe and the attached BMC water meter in addition to verifying fee-paying status and post-2018 timing (Appendix B, Table S2, PDF pp. 48-49), minimizing social desirability or observer bias despite unblinded community interventions. However, verifying installation timing (especially for unscreened replacement households), phone interviews for 1.5% of endline respondents from demolished slums, and midline petitioning-stage measures (application submitted, BMC visit, P-form received) relied on unblinded respondent self-report and multi-year recall.
confounding: Low concern for primary experimental estimates; moderate concern for exploratory moderator analyses: Two-stage cluster randomization (greedy covariate-matched block randomization of T2 across 76 slums and complete randomization of T1 across 152 slum clusters) produced good baseline balance across 17 covariates (Appendix M, Tables S6-S7, PDF p. 66), and covariate-adjusted weighted least squares models with block fixed effects confirm the unadjusted estimates (Table S14, PDF p. 71). Exploratory subgroup analyses (e.g., NOC land requirements, corporator partisanship/ethnicity) are observational across clusters and subject to unmeasured settlement-level confounding.
attrition: Some concerns (moderate risk): Over the five-year follow-up between the 2018 baseline and 2023 endline surveys, 38.5% of original baseline respondents were lost to follow-up (61.5% recontacted), primarily due to slum demolitions and temporary or permanent migration (PDF p. 22). Attrition regressions in Appendix N (Table S8, PDF p. 67) confirm no statistically significant differential attrition by T1 or T2 in either the full or eligible-lands samples, and 103 respondents from demolished slums were surveyed via phone, but pooling 2,444 post-treatment replacement households relies on within-cluster exchangeability and covariate imputation assumptions.
reporting_bias: Some concerns: The authors pre-registered the study on EGAP, transparently report null full-sample estimates alongside statistically significant eligible-lands subsample estimates in the abstract and main tables (Table 1, PDF p. 25; Table S18, PDF p. 74), and clearly label non-pre-registered mechanism and timing tests as exploratory. However, initial EGAP registration occurred in January 2019 after baseline data collection and during intervention delivery, the pivotal July 2019 amendment excluding 28 of 76 slums on forest, footpath, and saltpan lands was filed after intervention completion based on implementation learnings (albeit four years prior to endline data collection), and a February 2024 amendment specifying pooling of the 2,444 replacement households was filed after endline fieldwork concluded without reporting original-panel-only endline estimates (Appendix K, PDF pp. 63-64).
legal_measurement_quality: Strong: Legal and administrative eligibility rules were rigorously operationalized using primary judicial and municipal sources—including the 2014 Bombay High Court PIL ruling (Pani Haq Samiti & Ors. v. BMC), the 2015/2017 BMC Hydraulic Engineer's Department water policies, binding 2005 High Court prohibitory orders covering forest and saltpan encroachments, Right to Information responses from the Salt Department, and the 2022 BMC Water for All policy (Appendix F, PDF pp. 54-55)—paired with baseline GPS community mapping and NGO administrative logs classifying all 76 slums across 10 land-owning authorities and No Objection Certificate (NOC) regimes (Appendix I, PDF pp. 58-59).
outcome_measurement_quality: Strong: The primary water access outcome went beyond household self-report by requiring direct visual verification by enumerators of a physical municipal water pipe and an attached BMC meter (Table S2, PDF pp. 48-49), complemented by granular intermediate administrative milestones along the municipal connection process (application filing, BMC engineer site visit, P-form approval, and verified metered standpost connection).
where_found: Experimental Research Design & Empirical Strategy (PDF pp. 15-23); Experimental Results & Mechanisms (PDF pp. 23-34); Appendix B Variable Definitions Table S2 (PDF pp. 48-50); Appendix C Study Timeline (PDF p. 50); Appendix D Study Setting and Sample (PDF pp. 51-52); Appendix E Interventions (PDF pp. 52-54); Appendix F Ineligible Land Types (PDF pp. 54-55); Appendix H Qualitative Insights (PDF pp. 56-58); Appendix I NOCs (PDF pp. 58-61); Appendix J Research Ethics (PDF pp. 59, 61-62); Appendix K Pre-Analysis Plan (PDF pp. 63-64); Appendix M Balance Tests Tables S6-S7 (PDF p. 66); Appendix N Attrition Tests Tables S8-S9 (PDF p. 67); Appendix P-S Robustness & Additional Pre-Registered Analyses (PDF pp. 69-74).

study_design_identified: Non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel econometric policy evaluation using spatial reaction-function regressions (lagged OLS and spatial autoregressive/error MLE) and instrumental-variables (2SLS and LIML) regressions with urban-area fixed effects across harmonized Brazilian localities (1970–2000 decennial censuses)
why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates the determinants and causal population-growth/composition impacts of municipal public water-servicing policy across Brazilian localities over 1980–2000 using comparative panel/longitudinal fixed-effects regressions, spatial reaction models, and 2SLS/LIML instrumental variables. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel and instrumental-variables policy evaluations map directly to ROBINS-I.
selection_bias: Moderate risk — The main econometric sample includes 351 harmonized MCAs across 55 multi-locality urban areas that were at least 50% urbanized at baseline, avoiding post-treatment selection on outcomes, though restricting to baseline-urbanized localities in multi-locality agglomerations excludes initially rural fringe municipalities (<50% urban at baseline) experiencing rapid informal settlement growth.
measurement_bias: Serious risk for exposure / Low risk for outcomes — Exclusionary municipal policy is not observed directly and is proxied ecologically by the census share of 1–3 room houses connected to a central water network (which conflates intentional exclusion with capacity backlogs and non-migrant small dwellings), whereas demographic growth and household piped-water connection outcomes come from standardized IBGE Population Censuses.
confounding: Serious risk — Urban-area fixed effects, lagged covariates, spatial lag/error MLE, and 2SLS/LIML (instrumenting water servicing with porous geology and insolation interactions and housing supply with 1970 census/market-access variables) address major endogeneity, but plausible IV exclusion-restriction violations (geology/rivers affecting private water costs or growth amenities; persistent unobserved locality fundamentals), modest multi-endogenous first-stage strength (partial F ~ 13; F = 6.2 for untitled homes), and spatial weight-matrix sensitivity leave substantial residual confounding risk.
attrition: Low risk — Municipal splits and recombinations from 1970 to 2000 are harmonized into constant-boundary Minimum Comparable Areas (MCAs) using decennial census universes, with only a handful of localities having fewer than 10 surveyed small houses excluded.
reporting_bias: Moderate risk (no pre-analysis plan) — No pre-registration or protocol exists for this 2008 NBER working paper, and the text reports specification choices guided by specification tests (including selecting the 1991–2000 growth window over 1980–1991, choosing distance-to-Sao-Paulo and geology/insolation instrument lists based on strength and orthogonality tests, and favoring inverse-density weights where inverse-distance weights were insignificant); additionally, end-of-paper table/figure pages (PDF pp. 39–46, 48, 50) are unextracted in the PDF text.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate — Although the institutional narrative accurately describes Brazil's 1979 federal 125 sq m minimum lot-size statute, pre-1988 legal bars on municipal infrastructure provision in informal favelas and loteamentos, and 1999/2005 IBGE municipal zoning surveys, the econometric models do not directly code municipal legal rules or utility refusal ordinances over time, relying instead on realized census water connection shares among small houses as an indirect proxy for exclusionary policy.
outcome_measurement_quality: Strong — Household counts, household-head educational attainment, central piped water connections, and full servicing (electricity, central water, and central sewerage) are measured consistently across localities from official decennial IBGE Population Censuses (1970, 1980, 1991, 2000), though water quality, service intermittency, and affordability/tariffs are not observed.
where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 2); Section 1 Introduction (PDF pp. 3–6); Section 2 Urbanization and Public Infrastructure in Brazil, Data, Informal Sector, Servicing, and Land-Use Regulations (PDF pp. 6–14); Section 3 Conceptualizing Exclusionary Behavior (PDF pp. 14–20); Section 4 Determinants of Locality Infrastructure Servicing (PDF pp. 20–28); Section 5 Effect of Service Provision on Locality Growth and Population Composition, Instruments, and Results (PDF pp. 28–35); Section 6 Conclusions (PDF pp. 35–36); Appendix A Rent Hedonics prose (PDF p. 47). Note: Table and figure pages at PDF pp. 39–46, 48, and 50 contain only page numbers in text extraction.

study_design_identified: Quantitative analytical cross-sectional spatial regression study (multilevel negative binomial GLM across 31,383 Census block groups in nine U.S. states)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study is a primary quantitative observational cross-sectional analysis relating block-group municipal incorporation status and poverty rates to centralized water and sewer areal coverage at a single cross-section using multilevel negative binomial regression, without a longitudinal panel, before-after design, or quasi-experimental intervention/policy comparator; therefore, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching tool per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
selection_bias: Some concern (within the nine study states, all 31,383 Census block groups meeting explicit settlement-density criteria were systematically included, but the nine eastern U.S. states were purposively selected—limiting generalizability to western states—and block groups with low-reliability ACS poverty estimates [CV > 40%, >10% of block groups per state on average] as well as minor utilities lacking physical locations were excluded).
measurement_bias: Moderate-to-serious concern (Tier 2b approximates missing utility boundaries using municipal boundaries [e.g., 28% of MS POTWs], risking differential misclassification mechanically correlated with municipal incorporation status; Tier 3 approximates >1/3 of systems in several states as circular buffers from predicted area regressions; unlocated minor utilities are excluded and effectively coded as unserved; Florida relies on parcel-level imputations; and 2010 Census boundaries/demographics are combined with 2018 building footprints and multi-year utility shapefiles, with mixed block groups assigned a single incorporation status by majority area).
confounding: Serious concern (models adjust for population density, percent rural population, high poverty, and county/state random intercepts, but omit racial/ethnic composition despite extensive theoretical discussion of racialized municipal underbounding, as well as housing age and local soil/topography; furthermore, cross-sectional estimates face reverse causality/simultaneity because states such as Florida and Texas mandate water/sewer service provision prior to annexation, and random intercepts assume orthogonality between county/state unobservables and regressors).
attrition: Not applicable (cross-sectional spatial design using secondary data; however, non-trivial missing-data exclusions and imputations occur: >10% of block groups per state on average had low-reliability ACS poverty estimates [CV > 40%] and were excluded, 3.7% of CWS [n = 429] and ~6% of POTWs lacking physical addresses were omitted, and in Florida 27% missing drinking water and 7% missing sewer parcel records required deterministic imputation).
reporting_bias: Can't tell / Low-to-moderate concern (no pre-registration or pre-analysis plan is reported to rule out selective specification of density/buffer thresholds or covariate sets; however, full results across multiple model specifications with and without county/state random effects and poverty interactions are transparently reported for both sewer and drinking water outcomes, and compiled datasets are deposited in the Harvard Repository).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-strong (municipal incorporation status is rigorously operationalized using 2010 Census TIGER/Line and Census of Governments functional and class codes [funcstat, classfp], augmented by 240 m building-footprint rasters [>250 parcels/sq mi] to identify unrecognized unincorporated communities and spatial buffers [480 m for Islands, 1.6 km for Fringes approximating extraterritorial jurisdiction], contextualized with state annexation statutes; tempered by majority-land-area aggregation to block groups, a uniform 1.6 km ETJ proxy across states, and pairing 2010 municipal boundaries with 2018 building footprints).
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate concern (substantial effort compiled digitized service areas for 96% of active retail CWS and 94% of POTWs across study states, resolving overlapping polygons and EPA SDWIS mailing-address errors; however, reliance on municipal-boundary proxies [Tier 2b], circular radius predictions [Tier 3], parcel-level deterministic imputations in Florida, cross-dataset temporal mismatches, and areal coverage rather than verified household connections introduce heterogeneous measurement error).

study_design_identified: Non-randomized longitudinal pre-post (uncontrolled before-after) administrative panel evaluation across 53 Colombian municipalities comparing 5-year pre-update and 5-year post-update periods using robust paired-samples t-tests
why_tool_chosen: The study empirically evaluates the effect of a specific legal/administrative intervention—municipal cadastral updating under Colombia's five-year statutory mandate (Ley 1450 de 2011, art. 24)—on municipal fiscal extraction and water/sewerage utility outcomes across 53 municipalities by comparing 5-year pre-update (Periodo 1) vs. 5-year post-update (Periodo 2) longitudinal observations. Because it is a quantitative non-randomized comparative pre-post evaluation of a policy intervention across multiple jurisdictions rather than a cross-sectional survey, qualitative study, or pure doctrinal essay, ROBINS-I is the exact matching appraisal tool.
selection_bias: Moderate concern: Selecting the complete census of all 53 municipalities in three Colombian departments (Caldas, Quindio, and Risaralda) prevents arbitrary cherry-picking at the study frame level, but conditioning inclusion in the SUI aqueduct/sewerage (33/53) and IRCA water quality (42/53) analyses on database availability from 2005/2007 onward systematically restricts WASH analyses to municipalities that updated their cadastres in later years.
measurement_bias: Serious concern: Administrative SUI subscriber data exhibit acknowledged inconsistencies and extreme outliers in 20 of the 33 analyzed municipalities (PDF p. 17, fn. 3) and yield degenerate test statistics (t = -Inf, Cohen's d = NaN) in Table 6; aqueduct and sewerage coverage relies on an unvalidated author-constructed proxy dividing subscribers by cadastral parcels (mechanically linking exposure and denominator, with Formula 1 blank/omitted on PDF p. 7); urban and rural subscribers cannot be disaggregated; and IRCA water quality changes are confounded by varying annual health-authority sampling intensity.
confounding: Critical concern: Each municipality is evaluated via an isolated univariate robust paired-samples t-test (df = 2 or 3) comparing 5 annual observations up to the cadastral update year against 5 annual observations after the update year, with no unexposed control group, no adjustment for secular time trends or inflation in fiscal series, and no control for concurrent municipal tax statute reforms, arrears recovery campaigns, early-payment incentives, SGP indigenous-reserve/poverty formulas, or urban population growth.
attrition: Serious concern: Although the target population comprises all 53 municipalities in Caldas, Quindio, and Risaralda, missing administrative records and database start-date truncations reduce the analyzed sample to 33 of 53 municipalities (62.3%) for aqueduct and sewerage subscribers and coverage (with several included series further shortened from 5 to 4 annual observations), 42 of 53 municipalities (79.2%) for IRCA water quality risk, and 52 of 53 for SGP transfers, using complete-case exclusion with no sensitivity analysis.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis plan or protocol is reported, ~300 separate municipality-level paired t-tests are conducted at unadjusted alpha = 0.05 without multiplicity correction, Formula 1 is missing from the published layout on PDF p. 7, IRCA sample window descriptions conflict across PDF pp. 7, 16, and 17, and Tables 2, 3, 4, and 7 truncate rows at 41-42 municipalities while narrative text reports totals out of 52-53 municipalities; however, null findings on property tax, aqueduct coverage, and IRCA are candidly reported and highlighted in the abstract and conclusions.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate quality: Cadastral updating dates are drawn from official IGAC (2020) administrative records and contextualized within Colombian statutory mandates (Ley 1450 de 2011 art. 24 five-year updating rule, Ley 1176 de 2007 SGP water/sanitation allocation criteria, Decreto 416 de 2007, and Ley 1430 de 2010, alongside a minor typo citing Ley 715 as 2011 on PDF p. 6). However, the exposure is operationalized coarsely by placing the update year inside pre-update Period 1 without verifying fiscal implementation dates and by pooling 6 municipalities with asynchronous urban-only or rural-only updates against municipality-wide outcomes.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / Serious concern: Water and sanitation outcomes rely on national administrative registries (SSPD-SUI for aqueduct/sewerage subscribers and INS-SIVICAP for IRCA), but suffer from severe SUI reporting outliers in 20/33 municipalities, an unrendered proxy coverage formula combining SUI subscribers with cadastral parcel counts, inability to separate urban from rural utility access, and fluctuating annual water-quality test counts across years.
where_found: Study design, data sources (IGAC, DNP OEC/TerriData/SICODIS, SSPD-SUI, INS-SIVICAP), proxy coverage description, and statistical test (JAMOVI Walrus Robust Paired Samples T-Test) are in Metodología y Datos ([PDF Pages 6-7]). Municipality update cohorts and pre/post windows are in Tabla 1 ([PDF Page 8]), municipality-level t-test outputs and subgroup sample exclusions are in Resultados and Tablas 2-7 ([PDF Pages 8-16]), and data inconsistencies, SUI outliers (Footnote 3), proxy coverage rationale, urban/rural aggregation limits, and IRCA sampling gaps are in Conclusiones ([PDF Pages 16-17]).

study_design_identified: Mixed-methods process evaluation embedded within a 100-village cluster-randomised controlled trial (combining documentary review, repeated semi-structured interviews with NGO implementers, longitudinal structured observations of latrine construction, 10% random household and VWSC surveys across randomized arms, and within-intervention village-level linear regressions)
why_tool_chosen: The paper is a primary mixed-methods process evaluation that collects, analyses, and integrates both qualitative data (review of TSC/NGO documents and logs plus 6 rounds of semi-structured interviews with NGO staff and village motivators) and quantitative data (direct observations of household latrine construction, a 10% random household awareness survey across 50 cluster-randomised intervention and 50 control villages, a 10% random VWSC survey, and village-level linear regressions). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT is the designated tool for mixed-methods primary studies; the Quantitative randomized block (2.1–2.5) was selected to match the primary 50-vs-50 cluster-randomised arm comparisons (Figure 1, Table 2), while unadjusted confounding in the secondary within-intervention ecological regressions (Table 4) is explicitly captured in item 5.5 and the cross-tool confounding domain.
overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (narrative MMAT judgment; no numeric score computed — strong physical latrine observation and mixed-methods integration, but constrained by unreported qualitative analysis/quotes, unblinded assessment, incomplete fidelity and logbooks, unreported survey non-response, and unadjusted within-arm ecological regressions)
selection_bias: Moderate concern: 100 villages in Puri district were selected with government cooperation and randomly allocated 50:50 to intervention and control arms (sequence generation described in [6]), and 10% household (n=807) and VWSC (n=170) subsamples were randomly selected from village lists in Stata 13; however, sample sizes were logistically determined, survey non-response rates are unreported, absent household heads were replaced by any adult/member >16 years present at the visit, and process documentation missed 2 to 13 intervention villages on several mobilisation items.
measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate concern for latrine infrastructure status (assessed independently by trained enumerators via direct household inspection every 6–8 weeks using objective structural criteria, though complicated by strategic household over/under-reporting of joint-family counts); moderate-to-high concern for mobilisation fidelity and awareness measures due to unblinded enumerators, reliance on NGO motivator self-reports and incomplete logbooks, retrospective household/VWSC recall, and absence of direct measurement of actual latrine use.
confounding: Low-to-moderate concern for the cluster-randomised 50-vs-50 village comparisons of latrine coverage and household awareness (supported by identical 8% baseline toilet access and similar respondent demographics, though randomization mechanics are deferred to the protocol paper [6]); high concern for the secondary within-intervention village-level linear regressions (Table 4, n=50 villages), which are bivariate unadjusted ecological regressions that do not control for implementing NGO, village poverty/caste composition, severe flooding in 13 villages, political unrest, or local sand-price shocks.
attrition: Moderate concern / Can't tell for survey non-response: household counts observed for latrine coverage shifted slightly from n=4,699 in March 2012 to n=4,585 in March 2013 (partly reflecting inconsistent joint-family boundary reporting), response/refusal rates for the 10% household (n=807) and VWSC (n=170) surveys are not reported, and village motivator turnover plus local political unrest produced missing process data for 2 to 13 of the 50 intervention villages across specific mobilisation components.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: the parent cluster-randomised trial was prospectively registered (NCT01214785) with a published protocol [6], and implementation shortfalls and null associations are candidly reported, but no pre-specified analysis plan is cited for the process evaluation's 13 exploratory ecological regressions (Table 4) and qualitative findings are summarized narratively without systematic coding tables or verbatim quotations.
legal_measurement_quality: Strong-to-adequate programmatic operationalization: the paper accurately details the formal rules of India's Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) / Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan (NBA)—including BPL vs APL subsidy eligibility, the June 2011 subsidy increase from INR 2,200 to INR 3,200, VWSC composition mandates, Nirmal Gram Puraskar incentives, and election code-of-conduct halts—and directly tracks de facto street-level deviations from formal guidelines (such as extending subsidies to all households to defuse community conflict and omitting participatory triggering).
outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for latrine construction coverage and programme awareness, but weak/absent for latrine use: physical latrine completion was rigorously observed using explicit structural criteria (walls >1.5 m, door, unbroken/unblocked pan, functional pan-pipe-pit connection) and awareness was captured via translated and back-translated questionnaires, whereas actual latrine use/open defecation behaviour was not measured despite appearing in the study title.

Institutional/legal TSC rules and implementation fidelity: Results—Context, Intervention, and Fidelity assessment (PDF pp. 3–7, Table 1, Figures 1–2). study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional household survey (census-enumerated random sample of 593 analysed of 600 surveyed households across one notified and one non-notified slum neighbourhood, paired with GIS tap mapping, multivariable linear/logistic regression, and exploratory GSEM path analysis)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The empirical design is a single-wave quantitative cross-sectional household survey (conducted March–May 2016) comparing water access indicators and log-transformed LPCD across notified and non-notified slum neighbourhoods via multivariable regression and path analysis, without longitudinal follow-up or a quasi-experimental intervention evaluation design, matching the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies.
selection_bias: Low concern within the two target neighbourhoods, some concern at neighbourhood-cluster level: Within Matangrushi Nagar (1,285 households) and Indira Nagar (918 households), PUKAR conducted a full household census enumeration and selected 600 household codes via a random number generator, achieving 98.8% (593/600) analytic completion (PDF pp. 5, 7–8). However, purposive selection of only two out of Mandala's five neighbourhoods (~8,000 total households) limits broader intra-slum generalizability and creates a two-cluster comparison between exposure groups (PDF pp. 4–5).
measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: Primary water quantity (LPCD) was measured over two consecutive weeks using a previously validated physical container-enumeration method alongside direct GIS mapping and functional grading of community taps (PDF pp. 7–8). However, weekly container refill counts, water expenditure, collection time, and missed work/school relied on unblinded respondent recall to community-resident enumerators, survey questions did not distinguish piped municipal community taps from brackish borewell taps (Table 2 note b, PDF p. 14), and microbiological water quality was not tested (PDF p. 18).
confounding: Some concern (moderate risk of residual confounding): Multivariable linear and logistic regressions controlled for household size, monthly per capita household income, and religion (PDF pp. 8–9, 15). However, because only one notified neighbourhood (Matangrushi Nagar) and one adjacent non-notified neighbourhood (Indira Nagar) were sampled, neighbourhood legal status is spatially collinear with unadjusted settlement-level factors noted by the authors, including distance to the main road/river/landfill and historical arrival timing before vs after the 2000 cutoff (PDF pp. 4, 17). Additionally, 12.5% of households had 'Unsure' income modelled as an indicator category (associated with +36.1% LPCD, p = 0.012; Table 3).
attrition: Low risk / minimal missingness: Of 600 randomly sampled census-enumerated households, 593 (98.8%) provided complete data on key water variables and were retained in the primary analyses (PDF p. 8), though 74 respondents (12.5%; reported as 12 per cent on p. 18) responded 'Unsure' for monthly household income (Table 1, PDF p. 10).
reporting_bias: Unclear / no pre-registration reported: No pre-analysis plan or study protocol registration is cited. Primary log-linear and supplementary logistic (<=20 LPCD) regression results are reported transparently and consistently, whereas the GSEM mediation path analysis is explicitly described as exploratory, omits non-significant demographic covariates, and presents a simplified specification alongside mention of an alternative specification explaining up to 50% of the association (PDF pp. 9, 12).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / mixed quality: The statutory and judicial framework (Maharashtra Slum Areas Act of 1971 pre-2000 eligibility cutoff on state/municipal vs central government land, and the December 2014 Bombay High Court order in Pani Haq Samiti) is explained accurately and with strong institutional nuance (PDF pp. 4–5, 17). Empirically, however, exposure status ('notified' vs 'non-notified') was operationalized ecologically at the neighbourhood boundary level using resident 'barefoot researchers' ground knowledge rather than verifying individual household pre-2000 documentation or official municipal boundary records, despite the law conferring notification at the household level and 55.2% of households in the 'non-notified' neighbourhood holding metered electricity (PDF pp. 4, 7, 10, 17).
outcome_measurement_quality: Strong for water quantity and tap infrastructure; limited for water quality: Household water consumption (LPCD) was quantified across two consecutive weeks during peak summer scarcity (March–May 2016) by physically counting storage drums/jerry cans, recording standardized capacities, and multiplying by weekly refills—a method with established construct validity in Mumbai slums—and benchmarked against the WHO <=20 LPCD health-risk threshold, complemented by mobile GIS mapping of community taps (PDF pp. 7–8, 11). Microbiological contamination was not measured and community tap survey items conflated municipal piped taps with brackish borewells (PDF pp. 14, 18).

study_design_identified: Analytical cross-sectional observational study (secondary spatial linkage and two-level multilevel logistic regression of 2018 Zambia DHS household survey data, 2017 IBNET utility records, and 2018 NWASCO regulatory reports)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

measurement_bias: Some concern (household water interruption is retrospectively self-reported over a 2-week recall window without sensor/physical verification and omits outages lasting less than one full day; utility and regulator continuity [hrs/day] and consumption [LPCD] rely on unverified WSC self-reports with unclear operational definitions; DHS GPS coordinates are randomly displaced up to 2 km; and explanatory datasets span mismatched years—2015 GDP and GHSL, 2017 IBNET, 2018 NWASCO, and 2018-2019 DHS; PDF pp. 5, 8, 17-19).
confounding: Some concern (two-level multilevel logistic regression models controlled for household, cluster, and provider-level covariates or provider dummy variables, checked multicollinearity, and retained piped service type a priori; however, cross-sectional design prevents causal inference, backward elimination at p = 0.05 risks data-driven model specification, provincial GDP and cluster wealth are ecological proxies, and key confounders such as household storage tank ownership, 'voice', water collector gender, and blue water scarcity were unmeasured; PDF pp. 7-9, 18).
attrition: Low concern (cross-sectional secondary data analysis; no longitudinal follow-up, and item/cluster exclusions among eligible urban piped-water users were minimal: 47 households in 2 clusters missing GPS coordinates and 46 of 3,093 piped-water households [1.5%] responding 'don't know' on continuity; PDF pp. 6-7, Fig 2).
reporting_bias: Some concern (no pre-registered study protocol or pre-analysis plan is mentioned; multilevel covariate selection used backward elimination at p = 0.05 yet p < 0.10 estimates are highlighted as associations in the Abstract, Results, and Table 4, and Table 1 contains a typographical p-value error for the Provider chi-squared test [p = 0.93 on PDF p. 11 vs p < 0.001 in Table 2 on PDF p. 12]; mitigated by open availability of underlying datasets and supplementary code; PDF pp. 1-2, 9, 11-15).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate macro-institutional linkage but limited regulatory depth (correctly identifies Zambia's statutory regulator NWASCO and the 11 commercial Water and Sewerage Companies, spatially linking GADM district-aggregated provider coverage areas to DHS clusters and extracting 2018 NWASCO and 2017 IBNET performance benchmarks; however, regulatory metrics rely on unverified utility self-reports, exact utility network boundaries were approximated from administrative districts, and formal legal/tariff/rationing rules are not directly measured; PDF pp. 5-8, 17-19).
outcome_measurement_quality: Some concern (uses a standardised 2018 Zambia DHS binary question capturing >=1 full day without water from the main piped source in the prior fortnight and compares PCA patterns against NWASCO/IBNET hrs/day and LPCD; however, self-report is subject to recall bias and respondent absence from home, misses sub-24-hour intermittency despite utilities averaging 18.4 hrs/day, and is not directly commensurate with annual utility/regulator averages; PDF pp. 5, 7, 9, 17-19).

study_design_identified: Quantitative observational cross-sectional study (exploratory factor analysis and OLS multiple linear regression on municipal secondary administrative data)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes a single cross-section of municipal administrative data (2018 SNIS and 2017 IBGE) using exploratory factor analysis and multiple linear regression without random assignment, longitudinal follow-up, or a quasi-experimental policy/intervention comparator. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching tool.
selection_bias: High risk: Although the target universe is all municipalities in Minas Gerais (853 municipalities), unspecified boxplot outlier removal reduced the sample to 574 observations and missing self-reported SNIS variables further restricted regression models to 391 municipalities (45.8% of the state's municipalities), creating substantial non-random selection toward municipalities/providers able to report complete SNIS data.
measurement_bias: High risk: Both exposure and outcome variables rely heavily on self-reported SNIS municipal/provider declarations (explicitly acknowledged by the authors as potentially correlated with institutional capacity itself), combine asynchronous years (2017 IBGE technical staff vs. 2018 SNIS indicators), and apply Pearson-correlation PCA to binary dummy variables.
confounding: High risk: Regressions include only the four institutional-capacity factor scores and omit key municipal confounders (GDP/income per capita, urbanization/population density, municipal population size, regional location, and type of service provider such as state utility vs. municipal autarchy), alongside severe simultaneity/reverse causality between per-capita sanitation revenues/expenditures and service coverage.
attrition: High risk (missing-data / sample-loss equivalent in cross-sectional administrative data): Over half of Minas Gerais's 853 municipalities were excluded via unspecified outlier removal (down to n = 574) and listwise deletion of missing SNIS/IBGE fields (down to n = 391 in regressions), with missingness plausibly concentrated in lower-capacity municipalities.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern (Can't tell regarding pre-specification): No pre-analysis plan or protocol is cited; outlier-trimmed vs. full-sample sensitivity regressions are not reported, although null and counter-hypothesized findings (insignificant political capacity for sewerage and negative association for water supply) are transparently reported.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak: Municipal legal/policy planning instruments mandated by Federal Law 11.445/2007 (existence of a Plano Municipal de Saneamento Básico [PMSB] and Política Pública de Saneamento Básico [PPSB]) are captured only as self-reported binary dummy variables (1 = yes, 0 = no) in SNIS without verifying statutory enactment quality, regulatory enforcement, contract modality, or actual plan implementation.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-weak: Water supply, sewerage, and solid waste collection coverage rates are drawn from standardized SNIS percentage indicators, but rely on unaudited provider self-reports, omit sewage treatment quality/continuity, and restrict sewerage coverage to municipalities served with water without testing sensitivity to missing rural/informal populations.
where_found: Study design, variables, and statistical procedures are reported in Section 3 (Procedimentos metodológicos, PDF pp. 16-19 / journal pp. 447-450, including Table 1). Sample exclusions, descriptive statistics, EFA loadings, and robust OLS regressions are reported in Section 4 (Resultados e discussão, PDF pp. 19-25 / journal pp. 450-456, Tables 2-4 and Figure 2). study_design_identified: Repeated analytical cross-sectional household surveys (2016 and 2017 rounds analyzed via descriptive comparisons and separate cross-sectional multivariable and mixed-effects logistic regressions)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study analyzes two cross-sectional household survey rounds (2016 and 2017) using cross-sectional multivariable and mixed-effects logistic regressions within each survey year to examine associations between 15 demographic/WASH variables and household water FCR > 0.1 mg/L or caregiver-reported childhood diarrhea. As the authors explicitly note on PDF Page 11, the data come from cross-sectional surveys rather than an experimental or quasi-experimental intervention design (no DiD, ITS, RDD, IV, PSM, or longitudinal cohort follow-up), making the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies the exact matching tool.
selection_bias: High concern: The sampling frame was restricted to opposition-controlled areas of Dar'a and Quneitra where safe access was possible (with active-conflict communities deferred), within-community household sampling procedures varied across communities (map neighborhood division vs. random routes), non-response rates were unreported, and ~30% of surveyed households without children <5 were excluded post-hoc even for household water quality analyses.
measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern (mixed across measures): Household free chlorine residual (FCR) and pH were measured objectively with a Lovibond Colorimeter and DPD-1/phenol red reagents, and soap/water at handwashing stations was directly observed, but childhood diarrhea relied on 2-week caregiver recall with no standard definition of diarrhea provided, toilet functionality in regressions relied on self-report rather than enumerator observation, and the hygiene item question conflated market availability with household affordability.
confounding: High concern: Community Water Safety Plan (WSP) programming and water supply types were non-randomly distributed (e.g., 0% WSP coverage in Quneitra vs. 46.7%–50.5% in Dar'a). Although multivariable and sub-district mixed-effects regressions were run, covariate control relied on univariable and forward-stepwise p-value screening, omitted measured demographic confounders (household size, head age, female headship, number of children <5), and could not adjust for unmeasured security, power-supply, or infrastructure differences in cross-sectional data.
attrition: Some concern (cross-sectional exclusions and missingness): Longitudinal attrition is not applicable to repeated cross-sectional surveys, but household survey response/refusal rates were not reported, 29.8% (544/1,825 in 2016) and 29.2% (561/1,921 in 2017) of completed surveys were excluded post-hoc because households had no child under 5 years, and FCR measurements were missing for 74/1,281 (5.8%) analytic households in 2016 and 16/1,360 (1.2%) in 2017 without sensitivity analysis.
reporting_bias: Some concern / Can't tell on pre-registration: No pre-specified study protocol or analysis plan is cited (secondary IRB approval only), 2016 FCR regressions were omitted due to low FCR prevalence, forward stepwise p-value filtering selectively determined reported multivariable estimates, and text descriptions of Table 6 inconsistently labeled odds ratios <1 and >1 as protective or risk factors.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / indirect operationalization: Although the paper discusses UN Security Council Resolution 2165, the Whole of Syria WASH coordination architecture, private water-trucking markets, and regulatory governance via Water Safety Plans (WSPs), empirical measurement of institutional/regulatory exposure is limited to an unverified binary indicator of whether a household lived in a WSP-targeted community and self-reported reliance on piped network versus private trucked water, with no direct measurement of legal rules, vendor regulation, or household-level intervention fidelity.
outcome_measurement_quality: Mixed (adequate objective proxy for water chlorination; weak for diarrheal health outcome): Drinking water residual chlorination (FCR > 0.1 mg/L) was measured objectively at the household using a Lovibond Colorimeter and DPD-1 tablets (though microbiological parameters were not tested), whereas childhood diarrhea (<5 years in the past 2 weeks) was measured via unvalidated caregiver self-report without providing a standard case definition.

Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, AMSTAR 2 is the mandatory instrument for systematic reviews with an explicit search and screening process.
selection_bias: High concern — Despite reporting independent title/abstract screening (Section 3.1), the review capped Google Scholar retrieval at an arbitrary 20 articles (Section 3.6), excluded regional-language and grey literature without methodological justification, provided no list of excluded full-text studies, and included a 2019 study from Kenya (Agesa & Agesa [13], Table 1 item 8) despite eligibility criteria requiring focus on India's Jal Jeevan Mission.
measurement_bias: High concern — Data extraction was not performed independently in duplicate (Author Contributions p. 13 attributes data collection to a single author, with NVivo coding merely reviewed by co-authors, Section 4.1), per-study characteristics/sample sizes/outcomes were omitted from Table 1, no validated risk-of-bias tool was used (Section 3.9), and citation-mapping errors occur in Table 1 (both item 4 'Ranjeet Kumar' and item 10 'Kumar & Goyal' cite reference [9]).

reporting_bias: High concern — No a priori protocol or registration exists (AMSTAR 2 Q2 = No); English-only restrictions and exclusion of grey literature were acknowledged only post hoc as limitations (Section 8); study-level details promised in Section 5 (publication year, sampling, sample size) do not appear in Table 1; and unscreened external references ([25], [26], [31], [32]) are introduced into the thematic findings and conclusion.

study_design_identified: Convergent mixed-methods case study combining quantitative descriptive Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) pairwise-comparison questionnaires (N = 8 purposively sampled rural water utilities) with qualitative stakeholder interviews
why_tool_chosen: The study collects and integrates both primary quantitative descriptive data (structured Analytic Hierarchy Process [AHP] pairwise-comparison questionnaires analyzed via geometric mean priority vectors, consistency ratios, and consensus indices across eight RWS entities) and primary qualitative interview data (interviews with RWS entities, the Association of Bantul RWS, and the Village and Community Empowerment Office, explicitly citing Palinkas et al. 2015 on purposeful sampling in mixed-method research). Because there is no intervention/comparator (ruling out ROBINS-I) and no exposure-outcome analytical regression (making JBI Analytical Cross-Sectional ill-fitting), MMAT (Screening S1-S2, Qualitative 1.1-1.5, Quantitative descriptive 4.1-4.5, and Mixed-methods 5.1-5.5) is the exact matching appraisal instrument.
overall_rating: High methodological concern (per MMAT 2018 guidance, no numeric score is computed and overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component: qualitative component has 1 No [1.4] and 3 Can't tell [1.2, 1.3, 1.5] due to absent interview/coding protocols and unsubstantiated narrative claims; quantitative descriptive component has 1 No [4.2 survivorship selection bias in N=8 purposive sample] and 1 Can't tell [4.4]; mixed-methods integration has 2 No [5.1 rationale, 5.5 adherence to component quality criteria])
selection_bias: High concern — Purposive sampling restricted the AHP sample to eight active RWS in Piyungan Subdistrict meeting strict survivorship and performance thresholds (>=5 years operating, primary potable supply, >=50% connection capacity with expansion potential, and prior experience with alternative financial services; PDF p. 3, Section 2.4), systematically excluding defunct or struggling RWS despite interview evidence that several Bantul RWS had ceased operations, while omitting the total RWS sampling frame and respondent roles per utility.
measurement_bias: Moderate to high concern — Quantitative financing priority weights were elicited via standardized Saaty pairwise comparisons in AHP-OS with strong internal consistency (CR = 0.001702 and 0.00482; PDF pp. 3-4, Tables 1-2), but reflect subjective respondent preferences rather than audited financial or operational metrics, while qualitative interview instruments and coding procedures are completely undocumented (PDF p. 3, Sections 2.4-2.5).
confounding: High concern (not controlled) — Descriptive multi-criteria decision analysis (AHP) and qualitative case study of N = 8 purposively selected RWS in a single subdistrict with no comparator group, causal identification design, or adjustment for confounding contextual variables such as village income, hydrogeological source conditions, utility scale, or prior subsidy history (PDF pp. 3-4, Sections 2.3-3).
attrition: Can't tell / No information — Cross-sectional AHP questionnaire and stakeholder interview study; although data are reported for the eight RWS meeting purposive eligibility criteria, the paper provides no information on how many individual respondents or institutional informants were invited versus participated or whether any AHP pairwise matrices were excluded for inconsistency or missingness (PDF p. 3, Sections 2.4-2.5).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern — No study protocol or pre-registration is reported; top-level criteria and financing-alternative AHP results are presented (Tables 1-2, Figure 1), but sub-criteria pairwise comparison matrices/consistency ratios, questionnaire items, interview guides, participant counts, and verbatim interview evidence are omitted, and Table 1 contains inconsistent decimal formatting (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak — Legal and institutional constraints (specifically the lack of formal legal entity status of community-managed RWS preventing access to formal bank credit and forcing reliance on personal guarantees) emerge only as unquantified narrative assertions from interviews, without citing governing Indonesian legal instruments or systematically coding the legal form/registration status of the eight sampled RWS (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak — Water access, service continuity, water quality, and full cost recovery are not empirically measured; the study's quantitative output is subjective stakeholder preference ranking across four financing schemes (community, private, grant, and debt financing), paired with unverified narrative statements about pump/pipeline failures and consensus-based tariffs (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3).
where_found: Research aims and mixed data collection overview: PDF p. 1 (Abstract) and p. 2 (Section 1). AHP conceptual framework and financing alternatives: PDF pp. 2-3 (Sections 2, 2.1, and 2.2). Study site context (Piyungan Subdistrict, Bantul Regency): PDF p. 3 (Section 2.3). Purposive sampling criteria (N = 8 RWS) and interview/questionnaire design: PDF p. 3 (Section 2.4). AHP-OS pairwise comparison analysis and consistency thresholds: PDF p. 3 (Section 2.5, Picture 1). Quantitative AHP priority results and qualitative stakeholder interview findings on legal status, tariffs, and lifecycle financing: PDF pp. 3-4 (Section 3, Tables 1-2, Figure 1, Picture 2) and p. 4 (Section 4).

study_design_identified: Cross-national analytical cross-sectional observational study (Bayesian network probabilistic modelling and bivariate linear regression of 2004 country-level indicators across 101 developing countries)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study analyses a single-year (2004) quantitative cross-section of 101 developing countries to estimate conditional probabilistic associations (explicitly framed as a non-parametric alternative to regression models, alongside an OLS linear regression) between socio-economic, environmental, governance, and aid indicators and national water/sanitation coverage. There is no policy/intervention comparator or quasi-experimental design (ruling out ROBINS-I), no longitudinal follow-up (ruling out JBI Cohort), and no primary qualitative empirical data collection (ruling out CASP and MMAT; the paper's 'qualitative dimension' refers solely to subjective Bayesian probability theory and discretizing quantitative national indicators into low/medium/high classes). Therefore, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching instrument.
selection_bias: Moderate concern (sample covers 101 developing countries in 2004 while excluding developed countries, small states, and islands, but exact operational cut-offs for exclusion criteria, the full country roster, and item-level missingness proportions prior to Amelia II imputation are deferred to a companion paper rather than reported in full).
measurement_bias: High risk (authors explicitly warn that the compiled secondary dataset has strong heterogeneity of sources and collection methods and should not be used for quantitative interpretation; continuous indicators are discretized into 2 or 3 k-means classes causing information loss; WGI measures rely on subjective expert assessments).
confounding: High risk (single-year cross-sectional ecological design at national scale; 25 indicators are collapsed into 5 PCA composite pillars discretized into 2-3 levels, bundling governance effectiveness [WGI GE] inside the Human Development and Poverty [HDP] composite alongside GDP per capita, poverty, slums, health, and schooling so governance cannot be separated from economic development; income inequality [Gini] was omitted due to missingness; bidirectional/reverse causality is acknowledged).
attrition: Not applicable / Unclear (cross-sectional single-year 2004 national dataset with no longitudinal follow-up; however, item-level missingness across the 101 countries required Amelia II multivariate imputation and forced exclusion of the Gini inequality indicator, with exact missingness rates not reported in this paper).
reporting_bias: Some concern / No pre-analysis plan (no pre-registered protocol; variable reduction from 42 to 25 indicators was data-driven based on preliminary correlations/collinearity in Dondeynaz et al. 2012, DAG edge directions combine PCA with subjective author judgement, and detailed country-profile scenario reporting focuses selectively on Profiles 4 and 5, though error rates and sensitivity metrics are reported across models).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern (legal and institutional governance constructs are proxied only by economy-wide perception-based Worldwide Governance Indicators [WGI GE, which bundles rule of law, regulatory quality, and control of corruption; WGI PS AV; WGI VA] and counts/indices of international environmental treaty participation [Particip], discretized into 2 or 3 coarse k-means bins, with zero water- or sanitation-sector-specific statutory, regulatory, or municipal enforcement measurement).
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate-to-high concern (national water supply [WS] and sanitation [S] coverage come from the standardized 2004 WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme [JMP] benchmark, but rely on heterogeneous underlying national surveys, omit drinking water quality and service reliability, and are dichotomized via k-means into just two broad categories: WS 22-82% vs >82-100%, and S 9-58% vs >58-100%).
where_found: Study design, 2004 cross-sectional WatSan4Dev sample (N = 101 developing countries), and pre-processing/imputation are in Section 1 and Sections 2.1-2.2 (PDF Pages 2-3). Bayesian network methodology, k-means discretization, PCA composite pillar construction, and naive Bayes submodel structures are in Sections 3.1-3.2 and 4.1-4.2 (PDF Pages 3-9), with discretization bounds in Table A1 (PDF Page 19). Model fit, scenario simulations, bivariate WS-S regression, and five country-profile submodels are in Sections 4.1-4.3 and Tables 1-9 and B1 (PDF Pages 5-17, 20). Governance (WGI) validity debates, missing sector disaggregation, and omitted water-quality/cultural variables are discussed in Section 5 (PDF Pages 17-18).

study_design_identified: Quantitative cross-sectional household survey stratified by census-sector Social Development Index (SDI) with GIS spatial mapping and descriptive municipal policy comparison
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The empirical component of S182 is a primary quantitative cross-sectional survey (N=393 structured closed-ended 9-item questionnaires analyzed quantitatively across 7 socio-environmental census-sector strata, PDF Pages 8-10, 30). There is no qualitative data collection or thematic analysis (excluding CASP and MMAT—note that 'qualitative answers to be chosen from a previously determined set of alternatives' on p. 10 refers to closed categorical response options in Appendix I) and no quasi-experimental intervention comparator or longitudinal pre-post panel design (excluding ROBINS-I and JBI Cohort). Accordingly, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the exact matching tool.
selection_bias: High concern (disproportionate allocation of 393 questionnaires across 7 vastly unequal SDI strata ranging from 12 to 3,003 households—sampling fractions from 2.3% in Group 4 to 75.0% in Group 7—combined with random block selection, no documented household or within-household respondent selection rule, no sampling weights, an unquantified non-response rate, and a 12% error margin used for overall sample size estimation; PDF Pages 9-10, Table 2)
measurement_bias: High concern (outcomes rely on an ad hoc 9-item closed-ended subjective perception questionnaire without formal validity/reliability testing, operational definitions of Adequate vs. Precarious, or clear plan identification in Question 8, while the SDI grouping variable omits two unavailable education indicators from Cavallieri & Lopes [2008], borrows Rio de Janeiro factor weights, and relies on 2010 Census data despite an unreported multi-year gap to survey fieldwork; PDF Pages 8-10, 30)
confounding: High concern (census sectors were stratified into 7 composite 2010 Social Development Index groups capturing aggregate coverage, bathrooms per person, illiteracy, and breadwinner income, but zero individual-level respondent demographics were collected in the 9-item questionnaire and no multivariable adjustment, regression, or standardization was performed; PDF Pages 8-10, 12, 30)
attrition: Can't tell (not applicable to longitudinal loss to follow-up in a cross-sectional survey, though unit non-response/refusal rates and vacant-household counts were not quantified per group beyond noting that Group 7 fell below its target minimum due to refusals or empty households; PDF Page 9)
reporting_bias: High concern (no pre-registered protocol or survey fieldwork dates are reported, and internal numerical discrepancies appear between the narrative text/Figure 3 on PDF Pages 13-14 and Table 4 on PDF Page 18 regarding group-level sanitation service coverage and adequacy percentages, e.g. in Groups 1 and 5)
legal_measurement_quality: Weak (federal laws 11,445/2007, 12,305/2010, and 14,026/2020 and Guarujá municipal laws/plans including Complementary Laws 108/2007, 227/2018, and 228/2018 and Ordinary Law 4,367/2016 are accurately cited as institutional background, but legal/planning exposure is not analytically operationalized beyond an ambiguous self-report awareness item in Appendix I Question 8 that does not specify the plan names; PDF Pages 3-5, 14-15, 19-22, 30)
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (access, service quality, and improvement priorities across water supply, sanitation, solid waste/urban cleaning, and drainage are measured exclusively via single-item subjective resident perceptions in Appendix I without independent physical/technical verification, juxtaposed descriptively against 2010 Census and municipal SNIS coverage figures; PDF Pages 10, 13-18, 30)
where_found: Methodology: Area of Study, Group definition and sample size, Structuring and application of the questionnaires (PDF Pages 6-10, Tables 1-2, Equation 1); Results and discussion (PDF Pages 11-24, Tables 3-4, Figures 2-6); Final considerations (PDF Pages 24-25); Appendix I: Questionnaire (PDF Page 30).

study_design_identified: Cross-sectional quantitative questionnaire survey of 68 community leaders in subnormal agglomerations (Baixada Santista, São Paulo, Brazil)
chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
why_tool_chosen: The study's primary empirical component is a single-wave cross-sectional structured Yes/No questionnaire survey of 68 community leaders reporting descriptive percentages on access to water, sanitation, health agents, and social programs, with no experimental randomization (excluding RoB 2), no non-randomized intervention comparator arm or longitudinal pre-post structure (excluding ROBINS-I and JBI Cohort), and no qualitative coding, transcripts, or thematic analysis despite a passing citation to Triviños (excluding CASP Qualitative and MMAT). Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies is the matching instrument for quantitative cross-sectional surveys without a quasi-experimental design.
selection_bias: High concern: The Metodologia claims a four-stage stratified cluster/simple random sampling strategy across a universe of 14,079 households, whereas the Discussão states that the 68 respondents were community leaders who participate in monthly utility-community meetings, indicating convenience/institutional-interface recruitment of engaged intermediaries rather than a true probability sample of vulnerable households ([PDF Page 3 of 8], Metodologia e objetivo; [PDF Page 5 of 8], Discussão).
measurement_bias: High concern: Data were collected via an unvalidated questionnaire modified ad hoc into a binary Yes/No test because respondents felt embarrassed about partial literacy; each of the 68 leaders reported as a proxy for roughly 100 households; utility community agents and utility-affiliated researchers were involved in the governance interface being evaluated; and the authors explicitly note respondent fear of admitting land invasion ([PDF Pages 1, 4, 5 of 8]).
confounding: High concern: No confounding factors are identified for analytical adjustment and no design or statistical controls (e.g., multivariable regression, stratification, or cluster-adjusted estimation) are applied; all findings are unadjusted descriptive percentages ([PDF Pages 4-5 of 8], Resultados and Discussão).
attrition: Can't tell / No information: Although this is a single-wave cross-sectional survey rather than a longitudinal cohort, the paper provides no information on how many community leaders or households were initially sampled/approached, how many refused or were unreachable, or whether there was item-level missingness ([PDF Page 3 of 8], Metodologia e objetivo; [PDF Page 4 of 8], Gráfico 1).
reporting_bias: High concern: Gráfico 1 displays 29 numbered items running up to item 47 while omitting 18 intermediate items (05-06, 11, 14, 25-30, 32-35, 39-42) with no explanation; no protocol or pre-analysis plan is cited; raw numerators/denominators are omitted; and prose figures internally contradict both each other and Gráfico 1 (e.g., irregular residence described as a low percentage on p. 5 under Resultados yet 'na sua maioria' under Discussão; CADUNICO reported as not reaching 25% on p. 5 vs. 57% later on p. 5; SUS non-visitation reported as >75% vs. 90% on p. 5).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Legal and institutional exposures—irregular land occupation/tenure risk, utility social tariff registration, and enrollment in CADUNICO/Bolsa Família—are operationalized solely via unvalidated binary (Yes/No) self-reports from community leaders rather than administrative cadastres, tenure records, or utility billing databases, and the authors note likely underreporting of irregular tenure due to fear of confessing land invasion ([PDF Pages 4-5 of 8], Resultados and Discussão).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / High concern: Water supply coverage, water billing, trucked/spout water use, open sewage, sewerage connections, flooding, leaks, and household water-conservation behaviors were measured strictly through binary Yes/No leader perceptions without household-level survey verification, utility metering/connection records, or physical/environmental inspections reported in the data ([PDF Pages 4-5 of 8], Gráfico 1, Resultados, and Discussão).
where_found: [PDF Page 1 of 8] Resumo/Abstract and author affiliations; [PDF Page 3 of 8] Metodologia e objetivo (sampling frame, IBGE/IPVS stages, n=68 leaders out of 14,079 households, margin-of-error claim, Baixada Santista setting); [PDF Page 4 of 8] Resultados and Gráfico 1 (29 displayed Yes/No items numbered non-consecutively from 01 to 47); [PDF Page 5 of 8] Resultados and Discussão (monthly utility-community meetings, ad hoc modification to Yes/No questionnaire, fear of confessing land invasion, and conflicting percentage summaries).
