study_design_identified: Sequential explanatory mixed-methods study combining an observational quantitative panel/cross-sectional regression analysis of 4,218 PAMSIMAS Phase I villages (2014–2018 functionality data merged with PODES village survey data) with comparative qualitative positive and negative deviance case studies in seven Indonesian villages (FGDs, participant observation, and in-depth stakeholder interviews).
why_tool_chosen: The study explicitly employs a primary sequential explanatory mixed-methods design (Section 1, PDF p. 2; Section 2, PDF pp. 5–9), pairing quantitative non-randomized regression modeling of PAMSIMAS village functionality panel data with primary qualitative fieldwork (focus groups, participant observation, and in-depth interviews) in seven positive and negative deviance villages. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, genuine mixed-methods primary studies combining quantitative and qualitative empirical components are appraised with the MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool), using the Quantitative non-randomized block (3.1–3.5) alongside Qualitative (1.1–1.5) and Mixed Methods integration (5.1–5.5).
overall_rating: High methodological concern in quantitative component; moderate-to-low concern in qualitative and integration components (per MMAT 2018 guidance, overall quality is bounded by the weaker quantitative non-randomized component: 3 No and 2 Can't tell in items 3.1–3.5; 1 Can't tell in qualitative items 1.1–1.5; 1 No in mixed-methods item 5.5)
selection_bias: Moderate to high risk: Quantitative analysis excludes ~35% of Phase I villages (6,507 vs. 4,218 in Appendix C) without selection criteria or comparison of included vs. excluded villages, and excludes rehabilitated schemes by outcome definition. Qualitative purposive sampling of 3 positive and 4 negative deviance villages is conceptually justified via MIS/PODES data (PDF pp. 8–9), but exact village selection rules among eligible outliers and recruitment procedures within hamlets are not fully detailed, and positive vs. negative cases are geographically segregated (Java vs. outer islands, Footnote 21, PDF p. 13).
measurement_bias: High risk: In the quantitative component, both the outcome (facilitator-assessed water sufficiency, acknowledged in Footnote 10 as prone to positive overreporting because scheme status reflects on facilitators' own performance) and key predictors (unscaled CAP attendance headcount; binary dug-well proxy for water quality) suffer from measurement error. In the qualitative component, World Bank Water Global Practice staff/affiliates evaluated a World Bank-supported program without discussing researcher reflexivity or formal coding reliability.
confounding: High risk: Quantitative Poisson and logit models adjust only for village revenue per capita, a coarse binary dug-well indicator, and contemporaneous tariff collection (itself an endogenous post-inception mediator/outcome of functioning systems), omitting village population size (critical when exposure is raw log headcount of meeting participants), district/island governance fixed effects (e.g., Java vs. outer islands noted in Footnote 21, PDF p. 13), poverty rates, and engineering complexity. Qualitative outlier selection is further confounded by geography, with all 3 positive deviance cases in Java and negative cases reported as outside Java (though Banyumas is in Central Java).
attrition: Serious concern / Can't tell: Footnote 10 (PDF p. 6) notes 6,507 PAMSIMAS Phase I villages (with ~250 removed for data mistakes) and Figure 1 implies ~6,524 schemes (3,588 = 55% sustainable), yet the regression tables in Appendix C (PDF pp. 26–28) include only N = 4,218 villages (2,439 = 57.8% sustainable), leaving over 2,000 Phase I villages unaccounted for across the 2014–2018 panel without explanation of missingness or attrition.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis plan or study protocol is cited; Footnote 18 (PDF p. 9) refers readers to Appendix B for village-level qualitative details (water supply conditions, technology, beneficiary numbers), but the published Appendix B (PDF pp. 23–25) instead contains a Poisson vs. Logit comparison and omits the promised village case table; additionally, one of the four named negative deviance districts (Banyumas) receives virtually no empirical narrative in Section 2.3.2 (PDF pp. 13–15).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate to weak: Formal PAMSIMAS project rules (inception socialization, community cash/in-kind contributions, KP SPAMS water user group formation, rehabilitation grants, and central-to-village fiscal transfers) are described narratively, and qualitative fieldwork effectively distinguishes de jure participatory procedures from de facto street-level collaboration or elite capture; however, the quantitative exposure reduces institutional participation to a raw headcount of Community Action Planning (CAP) attendees unscaled by village population.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak in quantitative component, adequate in qualitative component: Quantitatively, village sustainability (consistently 'fully functional' across 2014–2018 without rehabilitation) rests on quarterly facilitator field visits coding whether 'sufficient' water reaches >80% of beneficiaries based on subjective household interviews without metered flow, microbiological water quality testing, or independent audit (PDF pp. 5–6, Footnotes 8 and 10). Qualitatively, week-long village visits triangulated physical system status, service continuity, and household water use across gender-separated FGDs and multi-stakeholder interviews (PDF p. 9).
where_found: Research questions and mixed-methods design overview in Abstract (PDF p. 1) and Section 1 (PDF p. 2); quantitative MIS/PODES data, functionality definitions, facilitator bias note, and Poisson regression results in Section 2–2.1 (PDF pp. 5–8) and Appendices A–C (PDF pp. 21–28); qualitative outlier sampling, week-long FGD/interview fieldwork methods, and positive/negative deviance case narratives in Sections 2.2–2.3 (PDF pp. 8–15); integrated synthesis in Section 3 and Figure 2 (PDF pp. 15–17).

study_design_identified: Qualitative participatory practice-research (action-research) single-district field case study drawing on stakeholder consultations, structured interviews with 8 sarpanches, direct/indirect observations, MoA documentary analysis, and descriptive baseline FSTP operational records
why_tool_chosen: The paper is a primary qualitative practice-research field case study ('As part of our practice research, we supported the district government pilot the approach. The data, consultations, and observations underpinning the experiment form the basis of our insights', PDF p. 1; Section 2.1, PDF pp. 3-4), directly matching the CASP Qualitative Checklist (which covers qualitative documentary/field and participatory case studies, including researcher-participant reflexivity in Q6). MMAT was not selected because the 2020 survey of 1000 rural households and the 10 km spare-capacity model are reported in separate publications ([13,14,31]) rather than as a primary quantitative empirical component with sampling/statistical methods in this paper, and only descriptive pre-pilot FSTP operational figures (2019-2020) are cited for planning context. ROBINS-I does not apply because there is no comparator arm or quantitative pre-post intervention effect estimation.
overall_rating: Moderate to high methodological concern (2 No and 3 Can't tell items)
selection_bias: High concern: Dhenkanal was purposively selected because it already possessed a donor-supported operational FSTP under Project Nirmal where the authors' organization served as knowledge partner (PDF p. 5), and sampling/selection criteria for the 8 interviewed sarpanches (out of 212 gram panchayats) and consultation participants are unreported (PDF p. 3).
measurement_bias: High concern: Qualitative data collection (consultations, structured interviews with 8 sarpanches, direct and indirect observations) lacks reported interview schedules, observation protocols, or coding procedures, and embedded advisor-implementers report no reflexivity safeguards (PDF pp. 3-4).
confounding: High concern (uncontrolled): Single-district participatory pilot with no comparator group and multiple concurrent institutional drivers, including prior donor-supported urban FSM capacity (Project Nirmal), SBM Phase 2 (2020-2025), the Odisha Rural Sanitation Policy (2020), and post-MoA IEC campaigns (PDF pp. 3, 5).
attrition: Can't tell / Not assessable: Engagement spanned 2019-2021 across ideation, consultation, and MoA signing, but no information is reported on non-participation or drop-out among consulted local governments, sarpanches, or post-MoA participating gram panchayats.
reporting_bias: High concern: Asymmetric reporting between baseline operational figures and post-intervention outcomes; the Abstract states that the partnership increased rural access to sanitation services within a short period (PDF p. 1), yet Results present zero post-MoA service delivery statistics, exact rupee tariffs, or verbatim stakeholder interview data.
legal_measurement_quality: Strong to adequate: Accurately specifies the constitutional, policy, and contractual framework—including the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments (Schedules XI and XII, Article 243ZD DPCs), DDWS letter S-18011/6/2021-SBM-DDWS (14 September 2021), Odisha Rural Sanitation Policy 2020, and the 28 December 2020 Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) across 17 gram panchayats—and critically distinguishes a non-binding MoA from an enforceable contract (PDF pp. 2-3, 6, 10, 12).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Pre-pilot baseline FSTP capacity (27 kLD, ~50% utilization, 13% rural share in Jan 2019-Feb 2020) is documented from municipal operational logs (PDF p. 8) and a 50% relative reduction in the rural distance surcharge is noted (PDF p. 10), but post-MoA claims of increased rural sanitation access (PDF p. 1) are presented without any post-December 2020 service-volume, tariff-level, or household-uptake data.

study_design_identified: Exploratory sequential mixed-methods study (semi-structured qualitative interviews in 8 southern Ontario First Nations communities informing a descriptive cross-sectional survey of 79 First Nations drinking water operators in British Columbia)
why_tool_chosen: The study collects and integrates both primary qualitative data (semi-structured interviews with operators and community leaders in 8 Ontario First Nations communities, analyzed qualitatively) and primary quantitative data (a structured questionnaire administered to 79 BC First Nations operators, analyzed via descriptive statistics in Microsoft Excel) in an explicit sequential exploratory design where the qualitative phase defined the survey instrument and both strands were integrated in the Discussion and Conclusions. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool) with the Quantitative Descriptive component (4.1-4.5) is the exact matching instrument.
overall_rating: High methodological concern (narrative MMAT judgment; no numeric score: sequential mixed-methods rationale and integration are clear, but overall quality is constrained by convenience conference sampling without a response-rate denominator, unvalidated self-report measurements with contradictory responses and a salary count error, high Ontario refusal rates, and minimal qualitative coding transparency)
selection_bias: High concern: Ontario qualitative interviews achieved participation from only 8 of 45 listed communities (8 of 28 confirmed to have a plant and operator) in relatively affluent, road-accessible southern Ontario 'best case' settings (PDF Pages 4-5, 17). The BC quantitative sample (n = 79) was a convenience sample recruited at an 'Operational Excellence Conference and Interactive Trade Show' without a known conference attendance denominator and under the unverified assumption that each respondent represented a distinct community (PDF Page 5), likely under-representing isolated or severely underfunded communities unable to send operators to a conference.
measurement_bias: High concern: Ontario interviews were recorded via interviewer handwritten notes rather than audio recordings due to operator fear of repercussions (PDF Page 5); BC data relied entirely on an unpiloted, unvalidated self-report questionnaire that permitted contradictory responses on job satisfaction (3 respondents checked both satisfied and unsatisfied; PDF Page 10), contained an internal arithmetic discrepancy in reported salary counts (50 + 16 + 33 = 99 reported responses out of N = 79; PDF Page 7), and omitted x-axis category labels in Figures 3 and 5 (PDF Pages 9, 13).
confounding: High concern (uncontrolled): descriptive exploratory mixed-methods study with no comparator group, stratification, or multivariable adjustment for potential confounders such as community remoteness zone, plant treatment complexity, system size, or band revenue base; quantitative analysis is limited to univariate counts and percentages in Microsoft Excel (PDF Pages 5-6, 14).
attrition: Moderate-to-high concern (cross-sectional nonresponse rather than longitudinal panel attrition): in Ontario, 17 of 45 listed communities could not be reached/confirmed and 20 of 28 confirmed communities refused or did not return calls (PDF Page 5); in British Columbia, the total number of conference attendees approached is unreported (unknown overall survey response rate) and item nonresponse was substantial on sensitive items such as salary, job satisfaction, paid vacation, and years of experience (PDF Pages 5, 7, 10).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: no study protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported beyond university ethics approval (REB# 13NV048; PDF Page 4). Although reported themes match the stated interview/survey topics, quantitative presentation suffers from missing category labels on Figures 3 and 5 (PDF Pages 9, 13) and inconsistent subgroup totals for salary on PDF Page 7 (summing to 99 rather than 79), and qualitative coding procedures and direct verbatim quotes from Ontario interviews are minimally reported.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak-to-adequate (contextual description strong, empirical operationalization weak): the paper accurately contextualizes Bill S-8 (Safe Drinking Water for First Nations Act), the AANDC 80:20 O&M funding formula, Band Council governance authority, and Isaac v. British Columbia (Workers' Compensation Board) (1994) (PDF Pages 3, 14-15), but empirically measures regulatory certification adequacy solely via unverified operator self-report without checking provincial certification registries, plant classifications, or band council records (PDF Pages 5, 7).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (indirect perceptual/self-reported outcomes only): no objective drinking water quality tests, drinking water advisory logs, infrastructure inspection records, or administrative payroll/turnover records were collected; outcomes were restricted to self-reported operator job satisfaction, perceived operational and governance challenges, self-reported certification status, and recalled historical operator turnover (PDF Pages 4-13).

study_design_identified: Convergent mixed-methods single-case study combining a cross-sectional descriptive household survey (n = 31 households randomly sampled from 379 cadastral lots) with qualitative thematic coding of open-ended survey responses (n = 15 household subset)
why_tool_chosen: The authors explicitly design and execute a primary mixed-methods empirical case study ('primary data was derived from the mixed research method of quantitative and qualitative research', PDF p. 5) combining quantitative descriptive household survey metrics (Tables 2-3, n = 31) with qualitative thematic coding of open-ended responses (Table 4, n = 15) integrated to classify household tenure security under SDG 11.1. Because there is no comparator arm or quasi-experimental policy identification strategy (ruling out ROBINS-I and JBI Cohort) and no analytical cross-sectional exposure-outcome regression (ruling out JBI Analytical Cross-Sectional), MMAT (2018) with the Quantitative Descriptive component (4.1-4.5), Qualitative component (1.1-1.5), and Mixed-Methods integration component (5.1-5.5) is the exact matching instrument.
overall_rating: Low methodological quality / High concern (per MMAT 2018 guidance, no composite numeric score is computed; overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component, with 'No' ratings on qualitative items 1.2, 1.4, 1.5, quantitative descriptive items 4.2, 4.4, 4.5, and mixed-methods integration items 5.2-5.5)
selection_bias: High concern. Although 66 lots were drawn via simple random sampling from 379 residential lots in Bamboo Settlement #3, only 31 households participated (47% response rate; 8.2% of total lots), and eligibility was restricted to lots on the 1994 registered cadastral plan, excluding post-1994 informal subdivisions or newer squatters. Authors note non-response stems from fear of sanctions and distrust of authorities, likely selecting for more tenure-secure households (PDF p. 5, Sections 4-4.1).
measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern. Although indicators were mapped to UN-Habitat (2018) SDG 11.1 definitions (Table 1, p. 6), data relied on an unpublished 35-item self-report questionnaire, substituted county-level census average income (County of St. George) for actual household income when calculating water affordability (Table 2 note, p. 6), reported persons per habitable room rather than verifying the 4 m2 bedroom floor-area threshold (Table 3, p. 6), and lacked physical/environmental verification.
confounding: High concern / Uncontrolled. This post-only single-settlement descriptive case study lacks baseline pre-upgrading data, a non-upgraded comparison settlement, or multivariable statistical adjustment; thus it cannot separate the effects of state squatter regularization and upgrading from resident self-built investments, central highway proximity, or local commercial amenities (PDF p. 4, Section 3; p. 8, Section 6).
attrition: Not applicable longitudinally (cross-sectional single-wave survey), but unit non-response at recruitment was high: 35 of 66 randomly selected households (53%) did not participate due to resident hesitancy (PDF p. 5, Section 4.1).
reporting_bias: High concern. No study protocol or pre-analysis plan is cited; Section 4 (p. 5) states that One-Sample Student's t-test confidence intervals were used for significance testing, but no t-statistics, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported anywhere in Results; zero verbatim quotes are reported for the qualitative analysis; and summary tenure and dimension-access figures contain major arithmetic contradictions (e.g., 14 + 2 + 10 = 26 reported as 25 on p. 7; households lacking clear tenure security reported as 5 on p. 7 and 25 on p. 8).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate for doctrinal context, weak for household-level empirical coding. Doctrinally, the paper identifies Trinidad and Tobago's State Land (Regularization of Tenure) Act of 1998 (cited inconsistently as Chapter 57:03 on p. 4 and Act 57.05 on p. 5), Certificates of Comfort (COC), the year-2000 COC application cutoff, and 30-year state-land adverse possession rules. Empirically, however, household tenure status relied on unverified self-reports, equated preliminary 'HDC engagement' (n = 7) with achieved tenure security, and reported internally contradictory totals across pages 7 and 8.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate. Improved water and sanitation were measured via self-reported facility type (on-lot piped connection vs. public standpipe; flush sewer vs. septic tank/pit, PDF pp. 5-6), without direct testing of water quality, daily per-capita supply (20 L/person/day), collection time (<1 hour/day), or septic tank containment safety within an active river floodplain, and water affordability (<10% of income) used an ecological county-income proxy rather than surveyed household income (Table 2, p. 6).
where_found: Study design, sampling frame (379 lots; 66 sampled; n = 31 respondents), Kobo Toolbox data collection, planned one-sample t-test, and Braun & Clarke reflexive thematic analysis in Abstract (PDF p. 1) and Section 4 / 4.1 (PDF pp. 4-5); legal/institutional context of Trinidad and Tobago's Squatter Regularization Program and State Land (Regularization of Tenure) Act 1998 in Section 3 (PDF p. 4) and Section 4 (PDF p. 5); indicator definitions and empirical results in Section 5 and Tables 1-4 (PDF pp. 5-7); tenure contradictions and contextual limitations in Sections 6-7 (PDF pp. 7-8).

study_design_identified: Mixed-methods longitudinal pre-post program evaluation combining household surveys (descriptive stratification and exploratory k-means market segmentation clustering) with follow-up community focus group discussions
why_tool_chosen: The paper collects, analyzes, and integrates both primary quantitative empirical data (pre- and post-rollout household surveys with N=843/287 in Mudaka and N=890/513 in Panzi analyzed via descriptive statistics and k-means market segmentation) and primary qualitative empirical data (follow-up community focus group discussions translated and analyzed to explain service utilization and cost barriers). Because it is a genuine mixed-methods primary empirical evaluation of a non-randomized community intervention (registered as NCT03536286) examining associations between baseline household socioeconomic profiles and subsequent Asili uptake alongside qualitative focus groups, the MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool) using the Quantitative non-randomized block (3.1-3.5) is the exact matching checklist under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
overall_rating: High methodological concern / Low overall quality (per MMAT 2018 guidance, no numeric composite score is computed and overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component: all five Quantitative non-randomized items are rated No [4] or Can't tell [1], three of five Qualitative items are rated Can't tell, and two Mixed-Methods items including 5.5 are rated No)
selection_bias: High risk / High concern: Although baseline household enrollment systematically sampled every third or fourth household with under-five children across mapped sub-regions in Mudaka and Panzi (PDF p. 3), follow-up analyses suffered severe selection/attrition losses (66% in Mudaka, 42% in Panzi), excluded households with missing baseline cluster variables or unknown village data (PDF p. 4), and provided no recruitment criteria, sample sizes, or selection procedures for follow-up focus group participants (PDF p. 3).
measurement_bias: High risk / High concern: Pre-specified primary child health outcomes (14-day maternal recall of diarrhea, cough, and fever, supplemented by medical charts) failed due to poor maternal recall in large households and inaccessible chart records and were omitted altogether (PDF pp. 4, 7). Follow-up Asili utilization and membership relied on unverified self-report afflicted by respondent confusion between 'user' and 'member' definitions (PDF p. 7), and focus group data collection/translation lacked documented rigor.
confounding: High risk / High concern: There is no unexposed comparison community and zero statistical adjustment for confounding. Quantitative analyses are restricted to unadjusted descriptive stratification and unsupervised k-means clustering of baseline wealth proxies analyzed separately by site (PDF p. 4), leaving associations between maternal education, household wealth proxies, and Asili service uptake wholly unadjusted (PDF p. 6).
attrition: High risk / High concern: Severe longitudinal loss to follow-up occurred in both sites—only 34% (287/843) of baseline households were retained in Mudaka (66% attrition) and 58% (513/890) in Panzi (42% attrition) due to local instability, displacement, and lack of formal addresses (PDF pp. 4-5, 7). No attrition balance table or statistical adjustment for missingness is presented, with attrition comparisons cited only as '(data not shown)' (PDF p. 7).
reporting_bias: High risk / High concern: ClinicalTrials.gov registration (NCT03536286) was retrospective as of April 23, 2018—nearly two years after August 2016 baseline enrollment in Mudaka and right before May-August 2018 follow-up (PDF pp. 1, 3). Intended primary child morbidity outcomes were excluded from Results (PDF p. 4), cluster variables without 'notable trends' (drinking water and roofing material in Mudaka; toilet type in Mudaka and Panzi) were selectively omitted (PDF p. 4), and attrition comparisons were cited as '(data not shown)' (PDF p. 7).
legal_measurement_quality: Weak / Low quality (private social-enterprise tariff/membership structure rather than statutory law): The intervention is an NGO/human-centered-design social enterprise franchise program (Asili) offering paid monthly memberships versus per-unit clinic and standpipe fees under community-level consent from the Mwami of Kabare (PDF pp. 2-3). Operationalization of contractual membership versus ad-hoc user status was compromised because respondents were confused about the difference between 'member' and 'user' (PDF p. 7), and exact monetary fee schedules were not reported.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak / Low quality: Clean water standpipe and clinic utilization were captured solely through self-report at follow-up with documented misclassification between 'member' and 'user' categories (PDF p. 7). Objective water quality/supply metrics were absent, baseline drinking water and toilet type variables were omitted from cluster reporting due to lacking 'notable trends' (PDF p. 4), and primary child morbidity outcomes were dropped entirely due to poor data quality (PDF p. 4).
where_found: Study design, setting, sampling, survey/focus group collection, dropped child morbidity outcomes, and k-means clustering methods on PDF Pages 1 and 3-4; site retention rates, market segmentation results, and focus group quotes on PDF Pages 4-6; attrition, rollout delay, recall, and member-vs-user misclassification limitations plus author analytic roles on PDF Page 7.

study_design_identified: Multi-method qualitative study combining a focused narrative document review (52 papers across 16 East and Southern African countries) with 10 purposively selected qualitative city case studies (122 published/grey documents and 34 key informant interviews in Harare, Kampala, Lusaka, and Nairobi), synthesized via manual thematic content analysis
why_tool_chosen: Although published under Frontiers in Public Health's 'Policy and Practice Reviews' rubric, the authors explicitly state they conducted a non-systematic focused narrative review rather than a systematic review (ruling out AMSTAR 2) combined with 10 primary qualitative documentary and key-informant interview case studies (34 interviews, IRB-cleared) analysed via manual thematic content analysis without any quantitative empirical study component (ruling out MMAT). The CASP Qualitative Checklist is therefore the exact matching instrument for this qualitative documentary and interview case-study synthesis.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (3 Can't tell items, 1 No item)
selection_bias: High concern (purposive positive-case selection): the desk review was restricted to post-2010 English-language documents without snowballing, and the 4 cities and 10 case studies were purposively chosen specifically because they had published reports of sustained initiatives with positive outcomes; furthermore, sampling criteria, stakeholder roles, and per-site counts for the 34 key informants are unreported.
measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: findings rely on secondary published/grey project documents and 34 key informant interviews without reported interview guides, recording/transcription procedures, or verbatim participant quotes in the article; insider affiliation of local 'focal person' co-authors and the EQUINET network with studied initiatives introduces potential social desirability and interpretive bias.
confounding: High concern for causal attribution (not applicable as a formal statistical domain in descriptive qualitative synthesis): no comparator sites or counterfactual designs were used, and observed social, material, and health improvements across complex multi-actor urban initiatives cannot be separated from concurrent municipal, donor, or socio-economic changes, as the authors acknowledge (PDF Page 14).
attrition: Can't tell / partially reported at initiative level: refusal and non-participation rates among approached key informants are not reported; case selection targeted already-sustained ('surviving') initiatives, though participant dropout is noted qualitatively in one case study (Warren Park 2 garden membership dropout after external funding ended and land lease fees became unaffordable, Table 3, PDF Page 7).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: although NYU IRB clearance was obtained, no pre-registered study protocol or coding codebook is cited, primary interview transcripts/quotations are omitted in favour of high-level synthesis deferring to external grey reports (refs. 27–31), and English-only published sources may under-report failed initiatives, though Table 3 explicitly tabulates implementation barriers alongside enablers.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak (descriptive secondary reporting only): legal, regulatory, and tenure dimensions—such as contested land lacking legal title in Hatcliffe, 5-year municipal leases in Warren Park 2, missing post-2006 legal mandates for neighbourhood health committees in Lusaka, county urban agriculture laws and a Special Planning Area / MoU in Nairobi, and Uganda's Ministry of Lands Housing and Urban Development community contracting guidelines—are summarized briefly from case reports without statutory citations, doctrinal verification, or systematic legal coding (Tables 3–4, PDF Pages 7–9, 12–14).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (unverified secondary narrative reporting): water, sanitation, waste, and health outcomes (e.g., pilot water-conserving toilets in 30 Epworth households, community water-testing attitudes, solid-waste briquette recycling in Bwaise, and general references to routine clinic data showing reduced communicable/epidemic disease) are reported narratively without standardized WASH definitions, microbiological/physical measurements, or baseline-to-endline quantitative data (PDF Pages 5–10, Tables 3–4).

study_design_identified: Primary qualitative case study (semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions, participant observation, and document analysis)
why_tool_chosen: Despite the journal banner reading 'REVIEW ARTICLE', Section 4 explicitly reports primary qualitative empirical fieldwork—semi-structured interviews (n=20), two focus group discussions (n=14), participant observation, and documentary triangulation—within an inductive constructivist qualitative case study design. Occasional percentages in Section 5 merely summarize qualitative interviewee agreement rather than constituting a separate quantitative survey component, making the CASP Qualitative Checklist (rather than MMAT or AMSTAR 2) the exact matching instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (5 Yes, 3 Can't tell, 1 No on Q1-Q9)
selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: purposive sampling targeted knowledgeable municipal officials, councillors, satellite heads, an academic, a Water Board representative (n=20), and community members in two focus groups (n=14) within Amathole District Municipality, but exact inclusion criteria, subgroup sample sizes, community recruitment procedures (including potential municipal gatekeeper influence), and refusal rates are not reported.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: triangulating semi-structured interviews, focus groups, field observation, and official municipal/Auditor-General documents enhances credibility, but interview and focus group guides, language/translation protocols, audio-recording/transcription procedures, and researcher reflexivity are unreported, and ad hoc percentages of respondent views are cited without explicit denominators.
confounding: Not applicable (qualitative case study with no counterfactual or statistical effect estimation): rival explanations for poor rural water access—such as post-2015 regional drought and dispersed rural topography versus municipal incapacity, unimplemented by-laws, and financial mismanagement—are discussed narratively across stakeholder perspectives rather than controlled quantitatively.
attrition: Can't tell / No information: single-cross-section qualitative fieldwork with n=20 interviewees and n=14 focus group participants; the paper provides no information on invited stakeholders who declined participation or withdrew during interviews or focus groups.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: no pre-specified qualitative protocol or coding framework is reported, Section 4 omits all details of how thematic analysis was conducted, and quotations plus occasional respondent percentages are reported selectively by theme.
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / descriptive only: the paper maps South Africa's constitutional and municipal water-governance framework (Constitution 1996 Bill of Rights and s. 229, National Water Act 36 of 1998, Water Services Act, Municipal Systems Act 32 of 2000, Municipal Structures Act, MFMA 56 of 2003, Division of Revenue Act, Free Basic Water policy, and the local Rural Household Connection Policy), but contains minor statutory citation inaccuracies (e.g., citing the Water Services Act as 'Act No 1997' and the Municipal Structures Act as 'Act No. 117 of 1997') and evaluates legal/policy implementation qualitatively through informant accounts rather than systematic legal or administrative coding.

study_design_identified: Mixed-methods Q-methodology study (combining qualitative concourse development, individual sorting interviews, and crib-sheet discourse interpretation with quantitative forced quasi-normal Q-sort rankings, principal component analysis with varimax rotation, and descriptive household socioeconomic profiling; n = 30 interviewed, 27 usable Q-sorts)
why_tool_chosen: The study uses primary Q-methodology, which explicitly combines qualitative empirical methods (concourse generation via documentary/forum review and key-informant conversations, individual sorting interviews and qualitative crib-sheet interpretation) with quantitative descriptive methods (numerical relative ranking of 25 statements on a -4 to +4 quasi-normal grid, intercorrelation matrix, principal component analysis with varimax rotation, statistical significance testing of factor loadings and distinguishing/consensus statements and descriptive household water-bill/income profiling). Because both qualitative and quantitative descriptive empirical components are core and integrated to produce the study's findings, MMAT (with the Quantitative Descriptive 4.1-4.5 block) is the exact matching appraisal tool.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (strong Q-set piloting, PCA factor analysis, and qual-quant integration, bounded by convenience/snowball sampling with single-workplace clustering, unreported recruitment nonresponse and 3/30 excluded sorts, absence of verbatim post-sort interview evidence, and unreported ethics/reflexivity)
selection_bias: High concern: Non-probability convenience sampling via personal and professional networks supplemented by divergent-viewpoint snowball sampling across three neighbourhoods (n = 30 interviewed, n = 27 usable Q-sorts); while purposive diversity aligns with Q-methodology aims, initial recruitment refusal rates are unreported and notable workplace/occupational clustering occurred (all 4 Factor 2 respondents worked at the same school in Mitchells Plain; Factor 3 skewed heavily toward affluent professionals).
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Subjective tariff fairness viewpoints were elicited using a piloted 25-statement Q-set with positively and negatively worded items on a forced quasi-normal grid (-4 to +4), mitigating acquiescence bias; however, household income and monthly water costs relied on unverified self-report (with several City Bowl respondents unaware of their bill size), language/translation procedures across multilingual neighbourhoods are unreported and post-sort qualitative explanations are not presented verbatim.
confounding: High concern (uncontrolled exploratory design): Observational Q-methodology study with no comparator arm or statistical confounder adjustment; neighbourhood, historical racialised segregation, occupation, household size and water bill levels co-vary in small subsamples (e.g. all Factor 2 respondents worked at one Mitchells Plain school), and the authors explicitly state the study cannot verify causal relationships.
attrition: Moderate concern / Can't tell: Single-visit cross-sectional data collection had no longitudinal loss to follow-up, but 3 of 30 interviewed participants (10%) yielded unusable Q-sorts and were excluded without reporting the reasons for exclusion or their neighbourhood profiles; additionally, 3 of the 27 usable Q-sorts did not load significantly on the five retained factors.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis protocol or registration is reported; quantitative ideal-sort scores and statistical significance markers for all 25 statements across all 5 retained factors are fully reported in Table 1 (with transparent criteria for dropping 3 single-sort factors), but qualitative post-sort interview data are selectively absent from the Results.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (contextual and normative operationalisation): Cape Town's municipal water governance instruments (increasing block tariffs, the 6,000 L/month free basic water threshold, indigent registration rules, Water Management Devices [WMDs] and the 2020 Water Strategy) are accurately contextualised from municipal and secondary sources and operationalised into 25 normative tariff-design statements, though formal municipal tariff by-laws are not doctrinally coded as an empirical treatment variable.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Subjective fairness perspectives are rigorously structured via Q-sort rankings and principal component analysis with varimax rotation (retaining 5 factors at p < 0.01 explaining 61% of sample variance), whereas physical/economic water outcomes are limited to categorical self-reported monthly water bills (Fig. 3) and qualitative rationales lack direct participant quotations.
where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction (PDF pp. 2-3); Past and present patterns of injustice (PDF pp. 3-4); Methodology: Statements for the Q-sorts, Participant selection and data collection, Analysis and interpretation (PDF pp. 4-7); Results, Table 1, Fig. 3 & Fig. 4 (PDF pp. 6-10); Discussion (PDF pp. 10-12).

study_design_identified: Primary qualitative study (qualitative documentary coding of 9 Ugandan laws/policies paired with 93 semi-structured interviews of local government technical and political actors)
why_tool_chosen: The paper explicitly states that 'Only qualitative data was used for this study' (PDF p. 1) and employs qualitative coding of 9 legal/policy texts alongside 93 semi-structured interviews analyzed deductively in QSR NVivo 12. Descriptive relative frequencies of coded excerpts in Table 3 summarize qualitative coding matrices rather than constituting a separate quantitative survey or econometric component; therefore, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the exact matching appraisal instrument rather than MMAT or JBI Cross-Sectional.
overall_rating: Low-to-moderate methodological concern (7 Yes, 2 Can't tell, 0 No across Q1-Q9; high research value on Q10)
selection_bias: Moderate concern / Can't tell: Although the sample of 93 local government actors is balanced across political (47) and technical (46) roles across 22 sub-counties in 3 districts (PDF p. 7, Table 2), the paper does not report how districts, sub-counties, or individual respondents were selected, how many invited officials declined, or how assistance from Whave Solutions field staff during 'research setup and fieldwork' (PDF p. 21) shaped selection within the 3 districts where Whave Solutions operates (PDF pp. 2, 19).
measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate concern: Interviews followed tailored semi-structured guides (S1 File), were conducted in English by two trained Ugandan research assistants with no prior exposure to service providers or respondents, and were deductively double-coded by two independent coders with good inter-coder agreement (Cohen's Kappa = 0.78; PDF p. 8). However, self-reported accounts of informal campaign borehole financing, 'facilitation' payments, and statutory compliance remain vulnerable to social desirability bias, full member-checking was not possible (PDF p. 19), and the role of Whave Solutions co-authors and field staff in interview guide input and validation was not critically examined (PDF pp. 2, 21).
confounding: Not applicable (qualitative design with no quantitative causal effect estimation). Contextually, all 3 sampled districts already had active Area Service Providers for several years and interviews took place in the year preceding Uganda's national elections, both of which shaped observed political and institutional dynamics as acknowledged by the authors (PDF pp. 7, 13, 19).
attrition: Low concern / Can't tell: Data collection consisted of single-timepoint semi-structured interviews; however, initial recruitment refusal/non-response rates (including during the two-month COVID-19 inter-district travel ban) are not reported, and high local government turnover plus COVID-19 restrictions prevented full post-interview participant validation (PDF pp. 8, 19).
reporting_bias: Low concern: The authors transparently report full coding definitions (S1 Table), frequency matrices across all regulative, normative, cultural-cognitive, and 'other' categories (Table 3; S2-S5 Tables), the complete interview guide (S1 File), and divergent/negative accounts across both political and technical officials, while appropriately withholding raw transcripts under IRB confidentiality rules (PDF pp. 1-2, 8-17, 20-21).

study_design_identified: Doctrinal-empirical legal-institutional compliance study combining Brazilian sanitation/transparency law analysis with descriptive administrative data (SNIS, IBGE MUNIC 2017) and a primary Freedom of Information (LAI / e-SIC) audit across 20 watershed municipalities (2016-2017)
why_tool_chosen: Despite self-describing as 'quali-quantitativa' in the abstract, the study conducts neither qualitative primary research (no interviews, focus groups, or qualitative thematic coding) nor analytical cross-sectional regression or quasi-experimental evaluation. Instead, it is a classic doctrinal-empirical hybrid / jurimetric-administrative compliance case study published in a law journal that pairs doctrinal analysis of Lei 11.445/2007, Decreto 7.217/2010, STJ precedent, and Lei 12.527/2011 with descriptive municipal sanitation indicators and a primary LAI/e-SIC audit across 20 Bahia municipalities, matching the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2.
overall_rating: Adequate descriptive legal-institutional evidence, weak for causal inference (structured non-validated judgment)
selection_bias: Low at the design stage (census of all 20 municipalities with urban headquarters inside the Bacias Hidrográficas do Leste), but moderate-to-high selection bias from non-reporting in quantitative service and investment analyses because municipalities without SNIS records or LAI responses are omitted from indicator averages.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: relies on standardized SNIS codes (IN015, IN056, FN024, FN043, FN053), BCB IGP-DI deflation, and IBGE MUNIC 2017, plus direct observation of e-SIC portal functionality, but depends on unaudited municipal/utility self-reporting (including contradictory initial vs. subsequent responses in Almadina) and omits municipality labels on the horizontal axes of Figures 1 and 2.
confounding: High risk / unaddressed for causal claims: the study uses unadjusted descriptive comparisons across municipalities and between 2016 and 2017 without accounting for municipal fiscal capacity, GDP, population size, service provider model (state utility vs. direct municipal provision), or physical geography.
attrition: Moderate-to-high administrative missingness/non-response: of the 20 BHL-headquartered municipalities, 13 (65%) lacked complete 2016-2017 SNIS sewage data; after primary LAI/e-SIC requests, 4 municipalities failed to respond, 1 reported having collection without recorded data, and 3 supplied only partial or single-year data, reducing analytic denominators to 12-17 municipalities across service and investment indicators.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: no pre-analysis plan or protocol; governance and LAI outcomes are transparently tabulated for all 20 municipalities (Table 2, Quadro 1, Table 3), but Figures 1 and 2 omit x-axis municipality labels in the published PDF and Table 1 displays 12 municipal rows despite the text citing 13 analyzed municipalities.
legal_measurement_quality: Strong doctrinal grounding and adequate empirical operationalization: accurately analyzes CF/88, Lei 11.445/2007, Decreto 7.217/2010, deadline-extension decrees through Decreto 9.254/2017, STJ tariff precedent (with one minor text slip writing STF on PDF p. 20), and Lei 12.527/2011 (LAI), and directly operationalizes municipal compliance via IBGE MUNIC 2017 PMSB status and primary e-SIC/physical LAI audit filings.
outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for descriptive benchmarking: uses standard SNIS sewage collection (IN015), treatment (IN056), and population coverage indicators for 2016-2017 alongside QGIS watershed mapping, but suffers from missing municipal data in 3-8 municipalities per indicator, unlabelled bars in Figures 1-2, and a discrepancy between the text ('13 municípios') and the 12 municipalities listed in Table 1.

study_design_identified: Comparative institutional and legal-historical case study (2003–2009) of two municipalities in Santa Catarina, Brazil, combining regulatory/statutory and litigation analysis, local weekly newspaper archives, municipal council minutes, and descriptive secondary administrative statistics
why_tool_chosen: The study is a comparative institutional and legal-historical case study (N=2 municipalities, Indaial vs. Itapema, 2003–2009) relying on municipal statutes, concession bidding notices, court rulings, monthly council minutes, weekly newspaper archives, and descriptive secondary utility/municipal figures. It conducts no primary human-subject qualitative fieldwork (interviews, focus groups, ethnography) and no quantitative statistical/econometric or quasi-experimental estimation (precluding ROBINS-I, JBI Cross-Sectional/Cohort, and MMAT), making the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the most appropriate instrument.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (strong institutional contextualization, jurisdictional specificity, and legal exposure definition; weak causal identification, confounding control, outcome harmonization, and coding transparency)
selection_bias: High concern: Purposive N=2 selection of contrasting post-CASAN municipal governance cases in Santa Catarina (Indaial shared management vs. Itapema privatization) involves strong baseline structural and political self-selection into each governance regime, and no explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria are stated for selecting auxiliary grey reports and local/regional media sources (e.g., Timbó's Jornal Médio Vale for Indaial).
measurement_bias: High concern: Comparative operational, financial, and coverage figures rely on heterogeneous secondary sources and mismatched years ('os dados partem de bases diferentes', PDF p. 12; FURB 2010 vs. SNIS 2001/2009 and Andersen 2009; CASAN vs. FGV 2008 and municipal reports) without standardized accounting formulas or inflation adjustments; service-quality problems in Itapema are documented via local press complaints without symmetrical press-complaint quantification for Indaial; and embedded cells of Tables 1–3 are absent from the PDF text layer (though key figures are stated in prose).
confounding: High concern: Major baseline structural confounders separate Indaial and Itapema—industrial textile economy vs. coastal seasonal tourism with floating summer population, population size (43,000 vs. 26,000), income/poverty and inequality, civil-society and river-basin institutional density, and political stability/ideology (PT participatory governance vs. impeached PFL mayor). While narratively described, the N=2 descriptive comparison cannot adjust for these confounders, and the authors note that socio-economic and ideological factors endogenously determined model choice.
attrition: Low concern / Not applicable at case level: Both selected municipalities (Indaial and Itapema) are tracked across the entire 2003–2009 study window and into the subsequent municipal electoral term, although longitudinal indicator completeness is asymmetric across cases (e.g., water/sewer coverage reported at 2001 and 2009 for Itapema via SNIS, versus a single cross-section from FURB 2010 for Indaial).
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern: No pre-specified protocol or systematic content-coding scheme governs the extraction of evidence from weekly local newspapers (2003–2009), monthly CMSA minutes (2004–2009), or grey administrative reports, creating risk of selective indicator and episode reporting across the two cases (e.g., 2% disconnection rate reported only for Indaial; water-shortage and sewage-leak press reports cited primarily for Itapema).
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-strong: Municipal governance regimes and regulatory exposures are concretely operationalized through primary legal and administrative instruments (Indaial Lei Municipal 3.218/2003, Lei 3.255/04, Convênio 001/04 with CASAN, CMSA and FUNSAM rules; Itapema Edital de Concorrência 003/03 and 004/03, court injunctions, 25-year concession terms, SMRC), with only minor citation/typographical slips (e.g., federal Lei 11.455/07 typo for 11.445/07 on PDF p. 4; court name imprecision in Note 19 on PDF p. 15).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Water supply and sanitation outcomes (network coverage, septic-tank share, R$/m³ water production cost, disconnection rate, tariff re-balancing, and social participation) are drawn from non-uniform institutional reports across different years without harmonized denominators, baseline-to-endline symmetry for both municipalities, or uncertainty/audit verification.

study_design_identified: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid policy implementation study combining a PRISMA literature review, a doctrinal review of Brazilian federal water/sanitation/Indigenous health legislation, and descriptive cross-sectional secondary administrative data analysis of Indigenous villages in Tocantins (SESAI/SIASI, 2019)
why_tool_chosen: This study is a doctrinal-empirical hybrid evaluating implementation of Brazil's National Health Care Policy for Indigenous Peoples (PNASPI) and basic sanitation laws in Tocantins by combining a review of 10 national statutes/ordinances and Scopus literature with descriptive secondary administrative tabulations from a 2019 SESAI report. Despite a heading mentioning primary quantitative and qualitative village data collection and a Data treatment paragraph mentioning chi-square and t-tests, the paper contains zero primary qualitative data and zero statistical analyses—ruling out MMAT, CASP, ROBINS-I, and JBI Analytical Cross-Sectional—and is not a standalone secondary systematic review (ruling out AMSTAR 2). The Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework directly fits this doctrinal-administrative hybrid design.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: High methodological concern / weak empirical rigor (strong institutional and jurisdictional context, adequate legal source identification with citation errors, weak empirical measurement, sampling, confounding control, and reporting transparency)
selection_bias: High risk: Although DSEI-Tocantins is described as covering 11,908 Indigenous residents across 160 villages and 9 ethnic groups, Tables 3 and 4 include only 5 ethnic groups (11,688 residents; 161 villages in Table 3, 160 in Table 4) while excluding Xambioá, Krahô-Kanela, Avá-Canoeiro, and Pankararu without explanation; legislative search selection rules are also unspecified (PDF pp. 4, 6, 8).
measurement_bias: High risk: Relies on secondary SESAI/SIASI (2019) administrative counts without operational verification of infrastructure functionality or water potability; the authors explicitly note severe differential surveillance under-notification of ADD in unserved villages, and the text conflates the acronym SAA ('Water Supply System' vs 'Alternative Health Actions') and confuses 51 unserved villages with '51 ADD cases' vs 131 in Table 4 (PDF pp. 6, 8).
confounding: High risk: Descriptive cross-tabulations of 2017 acute diarrheal disease (ADD) cases across village sanitation categories control for no confounders (e.g., village population density, remoteness, access to health posts/surveillance, age structure, water source quality, or actual treatment functionality), and planned chi-square/t-tests are never reported (PDF pp. 4, 6, 8).
attrition: Not applicable / High concern for incomplete administrative coverage: Cross-sectional secondary administrative compilation rather than longitudinal cohort follow-up, but 4 of the 9 ethnic groups in DSEI-Tocantins (~220 individuals) and 1 village in Table 4 (92 vs 93 WSS-only villages in Table 3) are omitted from the analytical tables without explanation (PDF pp. 6, 8).
reporting_bias: High risk: Methods state that primary quantitative and qualitative village data were collected and analyzed using chi-square tests and t-tests (p<0.05), yet zero primary qualitative data, zero chi-square/t-test statistics or p-values, and no bibliography/extraction table of the 44 PRISMA-screened Scopus studies are reported in Results (PDF pp. 3-4, 6, 8).
legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / Adequate with errors: Core Brazilian constitutional, statutory, and regulatory instruments (Constitution 1988, Law 9,836/1999, Ordinance 254/2002 PNASPI, Law 11,445/2007, Law 12,314/2010, Law 14,026/2020, Ordinance GM/MS 888/2021) are identified, but Table 2 mislabels Ministry of Health Ordinance (Portaria) No. 755/2012 as 'Law Nº. 12,651' (Brazil's Forest Code) and PNASPI compliance is evaluated solely via coarse village infrastructure counts (PDF pp. 4, 6, 9-10).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Sanitation coverage (presence of Water Supply Systems and Sanitary Modules) and 2017 ADD case counts come from aggregate 2019 SESAI administrative tables lacking clinical case definitions, potability testing data, infrastructure functionality metrics, and internal numerical consistency between text and tables (PDF pp. 6, 8).
where_found: PDF pp. 1-10: Abstract (p. 1), Introduction (p. 2), Methodology including Study area, Systematic literature review, Policy and legislative review, Primary/secondary SESAI data sources, and Data treatment (pp. 3-4, Tables 1-2), Results and Discussion including Brazilian legal governance and DSEI-Tocantins infrastructure/ADD tabulations (pp. 4-9, Figures 2-3, Tables 3-4), Conclusion and References (pp. 9-10).

study_design_identified: Doctrinal-empirical judicial docket-tracking multiple-case study (narrative procedural chronicle of three Public Civil Actions on municipal sanitation in Brazil, cross-referenced with secondary utility/news records)
why_tool_chosen: The study is a legal-institutional and empirical docket-tracking case study prepared by public law scholars analyzing judicial proceedings, court portal records, and concession documents across three sanitation lawsuits, without human-subject interviews/ethnography (making CASP Qualitative Checklist a poor fit for participant recruitment, reflexivity, and ethics items) and without non-litigated comparator units or statistical estimation (ruling out ROBINS-I, JBI checklists, and MMAT). The Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework directly evaluates its doctrinal accuracy, procedural/exposure operationalization, sampling from the 258-case universe, documentary measurement, and institutional enforcement context.
overall_rating: Strong legal-institutional docket documentation; high concern for selection, coding, and causal inference (structured non-validated judgment)
selection_bias: High concern: only 3 public civil actions were examined out of the 258 sanitation lawsuits mapped in Barcellos (2014); although described colloquially as random ("aleatória"), no randomization procedure or sampling frame is reported, all 3 cases are plaintiff-favorable rulings from Southern and Center-West Brazil studied by a 2016 UERJ undergraduate group, creating substantial risk of convenience or illustrative selection.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern: formal procedural trajectories are directly verified from official court portals, whereas real-world sanitation implementation is assessed via heterogeneous secondary sources (union, municipal, and concessionaire press releases) rather than standardized engineering or household-level data, and in Santa Maria compliance in December 2012 is inferred solely from the docket's archiving entry without independent physical verification.
confounding: High concern: the descriptive chronicle design lacks unlitigated comparator municipalities and cannot separate the effect of judicial orders from concurrent institutional, political, and financial drivers (e.g., the 2011 30-year SANESUL concession renewal in Aquidauana, 2015 municipalization politics in Santa Maria, environmental licensing via FATMA in Tubarão, and utility investment schedules), making causal assertions—such as claiming Tubarão's 2018 works occurred solely due to the lawsuit—unverified.
attrition: Low-to-moderate concern (incomplete docket access rather than case drop-out): all three selected lawsuits were tracked from filing (1999 or 2006) through judicial archiving (Aquidauana in June 2012; Santa Maria in December 2012) or ongoing execution (Tubarão through March 2018), but restricted public access to full party filings on the TJMS and TJRS websites created missing documentary evidence during the enforcement phase.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: no pre-specified protocol, extraction form, or coding rubric is reported, and the paper synthesizes unpublished 2016 undergraduate research chronicles in a personalized narrative style; however, the authors candidly report null/contrary observations, including Santa Maria's eventual compliance and Barcellos (2014)'s finding of no faster service delivery in litigated cases.
legal_measurement_quality: Strong: constitutional competencies, federal sanitation and procedural statutes (Law 11.445/2007, Law 7.347/1995, CPC art. 794, I), and case-specific litigation milestones (filing, first-instance sentences, appellate acórdãos, astreintes, prosecutorial motions, and execution/archiving orders) are documented with exact docket numbers, dates, and verbatim judicial excerpts across three courts (TJMS, TJRS, TRF4).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate: triangulation with local news and concessionaire announcements effectively exposes major gaps between formal judicial compliance and actual sewerage coverage in Aquidauana (15% coverage reported in August 2011 despite judicial extinction declaring full city sewage treatment) and Tubarão (zero implementation by early 2018 and a downscaled Phase 1 network), but relies on unverified secondary announcements and lacks standardized physical service metrics.
where_found: Research aims, case selection from Barcellos (2014), and narrative chronicle method are on PDF Pages 1-4 (Resumo, Abstract, Introdução, journal pp. 72-75); individual case chronicles and court portal/news triangulation are in Sections 1-3 on PDF Pages 4-16 (Aquidauana pp. 75-80, Santa Maria pp. 80-84, Tubarão pp. 84-87); comparative institutional synthesis and portal transparency findings are in Discussão and Conclusão on PDF Pages 16-20 (journal pp. 87-91).

study_design_identified: Philosophical-doctrinal essay combined with an institutional and regulatory single-case study (Uniontown, Perry County wastewater system and Alabama's Black Belt)
why_tool_chosen: Sections 1-5 present a non-systematic philosophical and historical essay, while Section 6 conducts an empirical institutional and legal-regulatory case study of Uniontown, Alabama using primary administrative enforcement dockets (ADEM eFile violations, 2008 consent decree, NPDES permits, Stop Work Order), USEPA diagnostic filings, engineering reports, collated SSO spill records (Figure 1), and author field observations/water testing. It has no comparator arm (ruling out ROBINS-I), no randomized or observational survey/cohort sample (ruling out RoB 2 and JBI checklists), no formal qualitative interview/ethnographic design (ruling out CASP and MMAT), and no systematic review protocol (ruling out AMSTAR 2), making the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the exact fit rather than NONE.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Weak methodological rigor for causal or generalizable inference (strong institutional context and jurisdictional specificity; adequate legal-administrative source documentation, exposure, and outcome definitions in the Uniontown case study; weak sampling, selection, measurement transparency, causal identification, confounding control, replication, coding transparency, and reflexivity)
selection_bias: High concern (weak): Alabama's Black Belt counties and the Uniontown wastewater treatment system were purposively selected as an illustrative model of systemic failure (PDF pp. 11, 15) without a defined sampling frame, case-selection protocol, or comparison against non-failing or demographically distinct utilities.
measurement_bias: High concern (weak): Primary empirical outcome data in Uniontown rely on municipal sanitary sewer overflow (SSO) self-reports from a facility with non-functioning flow meters (PDF pp. 14-15, 19) and on the author's own unpublished E. coli water sample counts (PDF p. 16) and personal site observations (PDF p. 14) presented without sampling, chain-of-custody, or microbiological assay protocols.
confounding: High concern (weak control): Descriptive single-case institutional narrative with no comparator arm or analytical adjustment to separate regulatory laxity from co-occurring structural factors including impermeable Kipling clay soils, severe county poverty and low local tax base, unpermitted industrial BOD/effluent dumping by Southeastern Cheese, and aging collection-pipe infiltration (PDF pp. 11-12, 14, 17-19).
attrition: Not assessable / Not applicable: The study is a philosophical-doctrinal essay paired with a single-municipality regulatory case study rather than a longitudinal cohort or participant sample subject to attrition, although missing volume estimates in early municipal sewer-overflow filings are noted (PDF p. 15).
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern (weak): The paper contains no Methods section, search strategy, or pre-specified coding protocol, and several doctrinal and empirical assertions cite unavailable sources including Dobbins unpublished manuscript/analysis (2019), Dobbins personal observations (2016-2018), and Dobbins unpublished data (PDF pp. 3, 6, 14, 16), creating substantial risk of selective evidence presentation.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (mixed): Section 6 anchors regulatory exposure in verifiable primary administrative and judicial records from ADEM eFile (2002 Notice of Violation, 2005 civil complaint, 2008 Consent Decree, 2008 and 2012 NPDES permits AL0063657, 2014 Stop Work Order 14-044-ld, 76 non-compliance citations, and Alabama water quality criteria §335-6-10-.09; PDF pp. 14-18, 20-21), whereas the comparative constitutional claims in Sections 1 and 3 rely on an undocumented unpublished manuscript/analysis by the author (PDF pp. 3, 6) and secondary citation of state code (PDF p. 16).
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Environmental sanitation outcomes in Uniontown rely on unvalidated, unmetered SSO volume estimates that shifted more than 100-fold across revised self-reports (PDF pp. 14-15, 19) and an undocumented grab-sample E. coli range from unpublished author data (PDF p. 16); county-level hookworm and straight-pipe figures are drawn secondarily from prior studies (PDF pp. 12-13), and no direct human health outcomes are measured in Uniontown.

study_design_identified: Primary qualitative case study combining semi-structured interviews (105 households, 25 community leaders, 7 leaders of thought, and 3 government officials), documentary/bylaw review, and exploratory field observation
why_tool_chosen: The authors explicitly design and justify the investigation as a primary qualitative case study using in-depth semi-structured interviews, documentary analysis, and exploratory field observations analyzed via grounded and axial coding (Sections 4-5, PDF pp. 7-9). Although simple response frequencies/percentages from the 105 semi-structured household interviews are tabulated alongside thematic narratives in Sections 6-7, there is no standalone quantitative survey or statistical analysis component that would warrant MMAT; therefore, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the matching appraisal instrument.
overall_rating: Moderate concern (2 No and 2 Can't tell items)
selection_bias: Moderate concern — Purposive quota sampling covered all 7 villages (14 households per village, n = 105) plus 35 leaders and officials, but within-village selection procedures and refusal rates are unreported, recruitment was mediated by village/clan heads who enforce communal sanctions, the requirement of household dependents potentially excluded elderly-only remittance households, fieldwork coincided with the festive return period, and women were excluded from deity-related surface-water questions.
measurement_bias: Moderate concern — Triangulation across voice-recorded semi-structured interviews, field observation, and documents strengthens credibility, and trained assistants/interpreters were used, but interview schedules are not provided, gatekeeper introductions via village/clan leaders risk social desirability bias regarding bylaw compliance, and water quality/safety was not objectively tested.
confounding: Not applicable / unadjusted (descriptive qualitative case study with no comparator group or statistical adjustment; socioeconomic gradients such as remittance-funded housing and underground storage tank capacity are discussed narratively without controlling for confounders).
attrition: Can't tell / low applicability (single-wave cross-sectional interviews with no longitudinal follow-up, though initial refusal rates among approached households are not reported and subgroup-restricted denominators appear for sacred-stream questions [n = 24 men] and women's water responsibility [n = 77]).
reporting_bias: Moderate concern — Thematic findings are clear, but qualitative depth across 140 interviews is illustrated by only four brief verbatim quotations, closed-ended percentage tabulations have occasional unclear denominators, and raw data/protocols are marked 'Not applicable'.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate — Communal environmental and water bylaws (mandatory household and junction stormwater ditches 'mgbacha ogwugwu', prohibition of boreholes/wells, mandatory August general assembly inspections and sanctions, and sacred-stream taboos) alongside statutory federal/state/local mandates are triangulated across community leaders, local officials, and community bylaws, though verbatim bylaw texts and formal enforcement records are not presented.
outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate to weak — Domestic water sources and coping practices (rainwater harvesting in tanks and erosion ditches, water sharing, stream fetching, and sachet/tanker purchases) are documented through interviews and visual inspection, but closed-ended response percentages lack the underlying questionnaire wording, minor denominator ambiguities occur (e.g., '96%, n = 77' on PDF p. 13), and no physicochemical or microbial water testing was performed.

study_design_identified: Doctrinal-institutional policy case study with narrative literature review, statutory/regulatory analysis, and descriptive secondary federal administrative data synthesis (SNIS, SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, SIOP)
why_tool_chosen: The study is a hybrid legal-institutional and descriptive administrative-data analysis of Brazilian federal sanitation governance—combining constitutional/statutory interpretation (CF/88 Art. 23, Law 11.445/2007, Law 11.107/2005, EC 95/2016, MP 868/2018, PL 4.162/2019) and institutional mapping with descriptive secondary statistics from federal databases (SNIS, SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, SIOP). It has no randomized or quasi-experimental intervention comparator (excluding RoB 2 and ROBINS-I), no analytical cross-sectional or cohort statistical model (excluding JBI checklists), no primary qualitative fieldwork (excluding CASP and MMAT), and no systematic review protocol (excluding AMSTAR 2), making the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the exact matching instrument.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: High methodological concern for empirical/causal inference (strong institutional and jurisdictional context, adequate legal/conceptual framing, weak sampling, measurement, coding, replication, confounding control, and causal identification)
selection_bias: High concern: Purposive, non-systematic selection of literature, official documents, and descriptive administrative data years (SNIS 2017; SIOP 2015-2019), alongside unexamined municipal coverage gaps (3,905 surveyed vs. 5,570 total municipalities in SNIS).
measurement_bias: High concern: Secondary administrative metrics from SNIS (2017), SIGA Brasil/SIGPLAN, and SIOP (2020) are presented in high-level charts without variable codes, budget rubric definitions, price deflation details (nominal vs. real expenditure in Gráfico 4), or data validation; Gráfico 2 labels solid-waste (PNRS) instruments while the text discusses basic sanitation plans, and the author cites Nirazawa and Oliveira (2018) regarding municipal sanitation data unreliability.
confounding: High concern: Structural confounders—municipal population size, rural isolation, low human development, weak local tax bases, and macroeconomic fiscal crisis—are discussed narratively via secondary literature, but no statistical, design-based, or comparative controls isolate federalist legal-institutional effects from socioeconomic determinants.
attrition: Not applicable / Can't tell: No longitudinal cohort or panel tracking of units over time; however, substantial unaddressed municipal non-coverage/non-response exists in the cited 2017 municipal sanitation plan survey (3,905 municipalities surveyed out of 5,570 total Brazilian municipalities).
reporting_bias: High concern: No research protocol, pre-specified indicator set, or systematic search/selection strategy is reported; administrative series, audit findings, and secondary studies are selectively marshaled to support the narrative argument.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: Core constitutional, statutory, and regulatory instruments (1988 Federal Constitution Art. 23, Law 11.445/2007, Law 11.107/2005, EC 95/2016, Portaria 171/2014 PLANSAB, Portaria 141/2005, MP 868/2018, PL 4.162/2019) and federal agency mandates are substantively described, though minor statutory citation slips appear (e.g., 'Lei n. 11.447/2007' on PDF p. 11) and specific decree numbers postponing municipal planning deadlines are omitted in Figura 1 and the reference list.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Outcomes (state-level treated sewage coverage, municipal management instruments, federal program proliferation, and 2015-2019 budget trends) rely on unvalidated secondary administrative aggregates without underlying numerical tables, indicator formulas, or adjustment for incomplete municipal reporting.
where_found: Methods statement in Resumo ([PDF Page 1]) and Section 1 Introdução ([PDF Pages 2-3]); theoretical federalism review in Section 2 ([PDF Pages 3-5]); statutory definitions, SNIS 2017 descriptive charts, deadline-postponement flowchart, and federal agency mapping in Section 3 ([PDF Pages 5-10]); fiscal rules, PL 4.162/2019 regulatory analysis, SIOP 2015-2019 budget chart, TCU oversight, and capacity-building discussion in Section 4 ([PDF Pages 10-13]); policy recommendations and data limitation caveats in Section 5 ([PDF Pages 13-15]); legal and secondary references in Referências ([PDF Pages 15-16]).

study_design_identified: Comparative legal-institutional and policy case study (doctrinal-ethnographic synthesis comparing statutory water reforms and customary water governance in Australia and East Timor)
why_tool_chosen: The paper conducts a comparative institutional, legal-policy, and legal-historical case study of statutory water sector reforms and customary water tenure across Australia and East Timor, analyzing primary and secondary legal/policy texts (including the Native Title Act 1993, 2004 National Water Initiative, 2004 East Timor Water Services Decree, and verbatim provisions of East Timor's 2012 Draft Water Resources Law) alongside published ethnographic research and donor evaluations. It fits none of the six conventional empirical checklists: there is no primary qualitative participant recruitment, interview guide, or qualitative data analysis protocol reported for this study (ruling out CASP Qualitative Checklist, despite a brief acknowledgment of ARC grants supporting Palmer's prior East Timor fieldwork), no systematic review search/screening methodology (ruling out AMSTAR 2), and no quantitative or quasi-experimental dataset (ruling out ROBINS-I, JBI, and RoB 2). Accordingly, per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1–2, the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is the exact matching instrument.
overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Strong institutional contextualization and jurisdictional specificity with adequate legal source accuracy, but weak empirical sampling, measurement, causal identification, coding, and replication transparency
selection_bias: High concern — purposive, undocumented selection of two national jurisdictions and illustrative subnational examples (e.g., Murray-Darling Basin, Katherine/Mataranka, Cape York; Baucau, Oecusse, Dili environs) with no explicit sampling frame or inclusion/exclusion criteria.
measurement_bias: High concern — the paper reports no primary empirical measurement protocol; claims regarding customary water governance and statutory implementation rely on narrative synthesis of secondary literature, donor reports (e.g., ADB evaluations), unpublished manuscripts, and unverified personal communication.
confounding: High concern (uncontrolled) — although historical, hydrological, demographic, and post-conflict contextual factors (e.g., North vs. South water development and colonial dispossession in Australia; Indonesian occupation, infrastructure destruction, poverty, and church opposition in East Timor) are richly described narratively, there is no counterfactual or analytical strategy to separate statutory reform effects from confounding conditions.
attrition: Not applicable — comparative legal-institutional and policy case study without an empirical participant cohort or panel sample subject to longitudinal attrition.
reporting_bias: Moderate-to-high concern (Can't tell) — no pre-specified study protocol, search strategy, or case/evidence selection criteria are reported, creating risk of selective citation of subnational examples and secondary literature aligned with the authors' normative argument.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate — key statutory, judicial, intergovernmental, and draft legislative instruments in both Australia (Mabo, Native Title Act 1993, 1994 Water Reform Framework, 2004 National Water Initiative paras. 52–54, draft Mataranka Tindal Aquifer Plan) and East Timor (Constitution, 2004 Water Services Decree, 2010 Third Draft National Water Supply Policy, and verbatim provisions of the 2012 Draft Water Resources Law) are situated accurately in institutional context, though several foundational legal sources rely on secondary legal commentary rather than primary legal citations and no systematic legal coding rules are used.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak — water access, governance recognition, and resource sustainability outcomes are assessed narratively through illustrative examples, secondary estimates (e.g., Indigenous-specific entitlements representing <0.01% of Australian water diversions), and anecdotal compliance observations rather than standardized, systematically collected primary outcome indicators.
where_found: Design and comparative scope located in Abstract (PDF Page 2) and Introduction (PDF Pages 3–4); funding disclosure in Acknowledgments (PDF Page 2); customary governance context in 'Customary Systems of Water Governance', 'Australia', and 'East Timor' sections (PDF Pages 4–9); legal, policy, and empirical outcome claims in 'Water Governance and Institutional Reform' subsections for Australia and East Timor (PDF Pages 9–16) and 'Discussion'/'Conclusion' (PDF Pages 16–19); sources in 'References' (PDF Pages 20–27). There is no standalone Methods section.
