study_design_identified: Primary qualitative participatory study using focus group discussions (FGDs) and stakeholder participatory co-creation workshops
why_tool_chosen: The Methods section explicitly defines and reports the research as a primary qualitative study following COREQ guidelines (PDF p. 3), relying exclusively on focus group discussions and participatory stakeholder workshops analyzed via qualitative framework analysis in NVivo 12, with no quantitative survey, experimental, or quasi-experimental component; therefore, the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the exact matching instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (1 Can't tell item on Q6 reflexivity; Yes on Q1-Q5 and Q7-Q9, with perceptual-only WASH outcomes)
selection_bias: Moderate concern: Purposive sampling across Korogocho and Viwandani NUHDSS sites selected childcare managers serving multiple village units and parents who were primary fee-payers with the longest center tenure, explicitly favoring dedicated volunteers likely to sustain multi-stage participation (PDF pp. 3, 5). More transient, newly enrolled, or financially marginalized parents and isolated centers are likely under-represented.
measurement_bias: Moderate to high concern: Data were gathered via moderator-led FGDs and participatory workshops, with self-evaluation FGDs conducted immediately after each workshop by the same research team (PDF p. 5, Figure 3). Without critical reflexivity or independent evaluators, participant appraisals of the co-creation process are vulnerable to social desirability and acquiescence bias, and WASH improvements reflect perceived potential rather than observed facility changes.
confounding: Not applicable (qualitative design; high concern if interpreted causally): As an exploratory qualitative participatory study without a comparator arm or quantitative estimation, confounding factors (such as baseline center resources or longstanding APHRC NUHDSS presence) are not controlled.
attrition: Can't tell / Some concern: Formative FGDs enrolled 200 participants (100 per settlement), and four participatory workshops each convened ~50 prior FGD participants across December 2021-May 2022 (PDF p. 5), but exact longitudinal attendance, refusal, or drop-out rates across the multi-session series are not reported despite lack of consistent commitment emerging as a negative theme (Table 2, PDF p. 6).
reporting_bias: Low to moderate concern: Reporting follows COREQ guidelines (PDF p. 3) and transparently presents both positive and negative stakeholder appraisals including resource, time, and commitment barriers (PDF pp. 6, 9-11), though the exact FGD and workshop topic guides are not provided in full and no pre-registered protocol is cited.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak for formal law / Adequate for informal norms: Formal legal instruments (non-statutory status of under-5 childcare services, UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, SDG 6.b/17) appear only as background framing (PDF pp. 2, 11). Empirically, the study operationalizes informal social accountability mechanisms (iSAMs)—role expectations, fee/supply agreements, informal inspections, rewards, and exclusion sanctions—through stakeholder consensus rather than coding formal legal or municipal regulatory compliance.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak for physical WASH outcomes (perceptual/anticipated only): No structured facility audits, microbiological/water-supply measurements, or child health assessments were conducted; meeting children's WASH needs was documented solely through participants' qualitative perceptions and anticipated expectations of the co-created process (PDF pp. 6-10, 12).
where_found: Study aims and COREQ/qualitative design in Abstract (PDF p. 1), Introduction (PDF p. 3), and Methods (PDF pp. 3-4); NUHDSS setting and purposive sampling of 200 managers/parents in Methods and Table 1 (PDF pp. 4-5); FGD/workshop procedures, quality control, NVivo 12 framework analysis, and ethics approvals in Methods and Figure 3 (PDF pp. 5-6, 13); thematic findings and verbatim quotes in Results, Table 2, and Figure 4 (PDF pp. 6-11); limitations and transferability in Discussion/Conclusion (PDF pp. 11-12).

study_design_identified: Primary qualitative study (focused ethnography from 2021-2023 combining semi-structured interviews with 24 informal street vendors and 6 public managers, field observations, and qualitative content analysis alongside municipal statutory/policy document triangulation)
why_tool_chosen: Section 2 explicitly states that the research adopted a qualitative approach using focused ethnography (2021-2023), purposive snowball sampling, semi-structured interviews with 24 street vendors and 6 public managers, and qualitative content analysis (Schreier, 2012), with no quantitative comparative or survey regression component. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, primary qualitative interview/ethnographic case studies map directly to the CASP Qualitative Checklist.
overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (8 Yes, 2 Can't tell, 0 No on Q1-Q9; valuable qualitative contribution in Q10)
selection_bias: Moderate concern — Convenience selection of a single municipality (Juiz de Fora, where the first author lived for over 20 years) and non-probabilistic snowball sampling of 24 central-area street vendors (out of an estimated 459 informal workers) and 6 public managers across 4 agencies. Snowball referrals through interviewees' social networks risk over-representing connected fixed-spot vendors relative to isolated itinerant workers, vendor demographics and refusal rates are omitted, and formal merchants, legislators, and civil society actors were not interviewed (PDF pp. 2-3, 8).
measurement_bias: Low-to-moderate concern — Qualitative content analysis used structured group-specific codebooks (Supplementary Material 1) and two-wave intra-coder verification achieving >80% agreement and Krippendorff's alpha >0.8, triangulated with field observation of downtown facilities and statutory texts; however, coding relied on a single coder rather than independent double-coding, interview guides and audio-recording/transcription procedures are not detailed in the main text, quotes are free translations from Brazilian Portuguese, and one participant code (CH_3 on PDF p. 7) is unexplained in Section 2 (PDF pp. 2-3, 7).
confounding: Not applicable (qualitative design with no quantitative causal effect estimation). Contextually, the study situates public-space WASH gaps within municipal fiscal priorities, procurement bureaucracy, heritage visibility embargoes, and street-level stigma toward unhoused populations (PDF pp. 5-8).
attrition: Can't tell / Not applicable — Focused ethnography (2021-2023) using one-time semi-structured interviews rather than a longitudinal cohort; snowball recruitment refusals or incomplete interviews are not reported (PDF pp. 2-3).
reporting_bias: Low concern — Presents convergent and divergent perspectives across municipal managers and street vendors (including vendors preferring paid clean facilities over unmaintained free chemical toilets and managers disagreeing over statutory scope and budget feasibility), summarizes limitations transparently, and points to codebooks and reliability procedures in Supplementary Material 1 (PDF pp. 3, 4-9).
legal_measurement_quality: Strong for qualitative legal-institutional analysis — Directly cites, quotes, and contrasts relevant international, federal, and municipal instruments, including UNGA Resolution 64/292 (2010), Federal Sanitation Law No. 11.445/2007, City Statute Law No. 10.257/2001, State-Owned Companies Law No. 13.303/2016, Juiz de Fora Municipal Sanitation Law No. 14.290/2021, the 2022 Municipal Water and Sanitation Plan (Decree No. 15.646/2022), Halfeld Park heritage decrees, and CESAMA's 2021 Bylaws, testing managers' claims against statutory text confining supply/sewage definitions to building connections (PDF pp. 1-2, 4-6, 9).
outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate for qualitative access and lived-experience assessment — Combines direct field observation and mapping of central-city public toilets, private pay-per-use alternatives (~US$0.50), and drinking fountains (Figs. 1-6) with street vendors' reported daily access barriers and coping strategies ('sevirologia'); no quantitative utilization rates, microbiological water/hygiene testing, or clinical health outcomes were measured (PDF pp. 3-8).
where_found: Study aims and legal framing in Abstract and Section 1 (PDF pp. 1-2); site selection, focused ethnography, snowball sampling, ethics approval, and qualitative content analysis procedures in Section 2 (PDF pp. 2-3); field facility observations, statutory/bylaw triangulation, and interview findings in Sections 3.1-3.3 (PDF pp. 3-8); synthesis (Table 1), limitations, and policy recommendations in Sections 4-5 (PDF pp. 8-9).

study_design_identified: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid / descriptive municipal institutional-data compliance study evaluating Human Right to Water availability, quality, and affordability across all 84 municipalities of Hidalgo, Mexico
why_tool_chosen: The study combines doctrinal analysis of international and Mexican Human Right to Water norms and municipal statutory tariff laws (Periódico Oficial decrees 55-170 of 2022; REPDA legal water-rights concessions) with purely descriptive municipal indicator accounting across Hidalgo's 84 municipalities. It fits none of the six conventional empirical checklists: there is no randomized assignment (RoB 2), no quasi-experimental intervention evaluation with a comparator group (ROBINS-I), no statistical association/regression analysis testing exposure-outcome relationships (ruling out JBI Analytical Cross Sectional and Cohort checklists), no primary qualitative fieldwork (CASP), no mixed-methods integration (MMAT), and no systematic literature search (AMSTAR 2). Accordingly, the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is the exact matching instrument.
overall_rating: Moderate-to-high concern (structured non-validated judgment: strong legal source accuracy, jurisdictional specificity, and institutional context, but weak measurement validity, coding transparency, confounding control, and causal identification)
selection_bias: Low concern for cross-sectional municipal coverage (includes the complete administrative universe of all 84 municipalities in Hidalgo), but moderate concern for longitudinal affordability estimates (Table 4 uses only CAASIM tariffs covering 15 municipalities and a national rather than state/municipal bottled-water expenditure survey mean).
measurement_bias: High risk: municipal per-capita water availability (DAmh) divides legally concessioned REPDA volumes by population without accounting for distribution leakage, unused concessions, or intermittent rationing (tandeo), yielding paradoxically high supply estimates in rural municipalities with high proportions of unpiped dwellings (e.g., Pacula 361 L/h/d with 23% unpiped; Huautla 122 L/h/d with 34.8%-36% unpiped). Affordability (GPAHmh) combines a uniform 2017 national bottled-water spending average (51.74 MXN/week) with imputed 1- and 2-minimum-wage incomes rather than observed municipal household spending and incomes, alongside denominator inconsistencies in Table 4.
confounding: High risk (uncontrolled): purely descriptive municipal ratios and aggregate time series with no statistical adjustment or stratification for municipal income distribution, informal sector earnings, household size heterogeneity around the 3.7 mean, rural spring/well self-supply, climate, or topography.
attrition: Low concern / Not applicable for cross-sectional municipal indicators (complete census of all 84 municipalities in Hidalgo); however, longitudinal 2013-2022 tariff tracking in Table 4 is restricted to the 15-municipality CAASIM utility rather than all 84 municipalities.
reporting_bias: Some concern / Can't tell: no pre-registered protocol or analysis plan exists; municipal availability estimates are fully reported for all 84 municipalities (Tables 1-2), but municipality-specific tariff and expenditure figures are reported only as grouped map intervals (Map 4) rather than exact values, and internal numerical discrepancies on PDF pp. 10 and 16 (Table 4) are unacknowledged.
legal_measurement_quality: Adequate-to-strong doctrinal source identification (accurate citation of UN General Comment No. 15, UNGA Res. 64/292, Mexican Constitution Arts. 4 and 115, Ley de Aguas Nacionales, REPDA water-rights registry, and Hidalgo Periódico Oficial municipal tariff decrees 55-170 of 2022), but weak-to-moderate empirical operationalization because tariff-coding rules across heterogeneous municipal decrees are undocumented and formal REPDA legal concession volumes are conflated with actual physical household water delivery.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate: relies on synthetic ecological/simulated household indicators (concessioned liters per inhabitant and simulated minimum-wage expenditure shares) and basin-level CONAGUA water-quality traffic lights rather than direct household-level measurement of tap-water continuity, potability, health outcomes, or out-of-pocket water expenditure.
where_found: Study design and objectives on [PDF Pages 1, 4 of 21] (pp. 169, 172); international and Mexican constitutional/statutory legal framework on [PDF Pages 4-7 of 21] (pp. 172-175); empirical data sources, algebraic formulas (DAmh, GPAHmh), and hypothesis in Materiales y métodos on [PDF Pages 7-8 of 21] (pp. 175-176); hydrological, water-quality, and institutional context on [PDF Pages 8-13 of 21] (pp. 176-181); municipal availability and affordability estimates (Tables 1-4, Map 4) on [PDF Pages 13-17 of 21] (pp. 181-185); policy conclusions and database URLs on [PDF Pages 17-21 of 21] (pp. 185-189).

study_design_identified: Deterministic game-theoretic agent-based simulation model (ABM) parameterized and calibrated using secondary summary scores from five previously published urban case studies in Kenya and Ghana
why_tool_chosen: This article develops and runs a deterministic computational simulation—an agent-based model (ABM) in NetLogo v4.1.3 built on game-theoretic payoff matrices and bounded-rational learning equations—parameterized and calibrated against pre-existing aggregate ordinal scores from prior publications (Bellaubi and Visscher 2014, 2016; GII 2011; TIK 2011). It reports no primary empirical human-subjects sampling, survey/cohort data collection, quasi-experimental policy evaluation, primary qualitative fieldwork, mixed-methods primary integration, systematic literature search, or doctrinal/jurimetric analysis of primary legal texts. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, forcing a primary empirical checklist or the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework onto a computational simulation model is inappropriate, so NONE is selected.
overall_rating: NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)
selection_bias: High concern in secondary empirical inputs (not directly applicable to deterministic simulation mechanics): calibration relies on five pre-existing urban case-study neighbourhoods (Old Town in Mombasa, Migosi in Kisumu, and Kangemi in Nairobi, Kenya; Madina and Nima in Accra, Ghana) from Bellaubi and Visscher (2014), with no sampling frame, site-selection rationale, or household/informant recruitment criteria reported in this article.
measurement_bias: High concern: governance inputs (transparency, accountability, participation [TAP], and social cost) and WSD performance benchmarks rely on secondary 'participatory scoring' imported from prior reports (GII 2011; TIK 2011; Bellaubi and Visscher 2014) plus 'Bellaubi (personal observation)' (PDF p. 3), with no primary measurement protocols, respondent counts, or inter-rater reliability reported here; additionally, Table 3 (PDF p. 3) swaps the text definitions and unit scales of Continuity and Coverage, and Table 5 (PDF p. 7) states a maximum indicator value of 3 (total 15) despite Table 3 defining 0-2 scales (maximum total 10).
confounding: High concern: the deterministic simulation attributes cross-system differences in water service delivery (WSD) performance solely to principal-agent game equilibria and calibrates a single free parameter C (1.6 in Kenya; 1.8 in Ghana) against country-average performance scores, omitting infrastructural, hydrological, fiscal, tariff, and demographic confounders between Kenyan and Ghanaian urban service areas.
attrition: Not applicable: the study runs a deterministic 12-month computational simulation in NetLogo v4.1.3 using static secondary summary inputs rather than following a cohort or panel of human participants over time.
reporting_bias: Moderate concern: model code and ODD documentation are deposited externally in the CoMSES Computational Model Library (Bellaubi et al. 2014), supporting computational inspectability, but the paper reports no pre-specified analysis/validation plan, no sensitivity analysis to ad hoc payoff equations (e.g., T = 1.5 - accountability; S = (participation / C) - social cost), and calibrates one free parameter per country against a single country-level mean percentage.
legal_measurement_quality: Weak: regulatory and contractual frameworks in Kenya (MWI, WASREB, municipal corporate utilities) and Ghana (MHWW, PURC, GWCL, AVRL management contract) are stylized into dyadic principal-agent links scored on a coarse 3-point ordinal transparency scale (0, 0.5, 1 for written rules) and accountability scale without citing specific statutes, regulations, licenses, or contract provisions.
outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (secondary coarse benchmark): WSD performance is imported from five previously studied urban neighbourhoods as a 5-indicator ordinal WSDA score (continuity, quality, coverage, affordability, quantity; Tables 3 and 5) containing internal definitional/scale discrepancies between Tables 3 and 5 and collapsed into unweighted country means (23.3% in Kenya; 16.6% in Ghana) to calibrate simulated game payoffs.
where_found: Abstract & Introduction (PDF pp. 1-2); Research Methodology & secondary case-study sourcing (PDF p. 2); Principal-agent TAP, management practice, and WSDA indicator definitions and Kenya/Ghana actor mappings (PDF pp. 2-7, Tables 1-5, Figs. 1-2); NetLogo v4.1.3 ABM specification, payoff equations, and sequential decision/learning rules (PDF pp. 4, 7-8, Figs. 3-4, Table 6); Single principal-agent equilibrium dynamics, calibration of parameter C, and country simulation outputs (PDF pp. 9-12, Figs. 5-10, Table 7); Discussion and model limitations (PDF p. 12).
